Proves the fix with evidence (logical reads before/after)

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'nobody changed the code' rules out a regression, missing that growing data volume is itself the real cause
Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with STATISTICS TIME/IO or direct timing, not assumption
Cursor cost scales with fixed per-row overhead that compounds as row counts grow month over month
Check the cursor's own driving query for separate degradation (stale stats, scan vs. seek)
Rewrite as one set-based UPDATE ... FROM statement
Validate the rewrite produces identical results before replacing the original in production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a concrete way to confirm the cursor is the bottleneck
Explains why cursor cost compounds as data grows
Correctly rewrites the loop as a set-based UPDATE
Addresses validation before production rollout

questions.title: Blocking Caused by a Missing Index, Not a Bug in the Code
questions.prompt: Every weekday around 10 AM, the order-entry application starts timing out for a few minutes. SQL Server's Activity Monitor shows dozens of INSERT statements from the app blocked behind a single SELECT from a management report that joins Orders to OrderLines. The report query and the INSERT statements haven't changed in months. sys.dm_tran_locks shows the report query holding a table-level (not row-level) lock on OrderLines. Diagnose why a plain SELECT is blocking INSERTs this badly, and fix it.
questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, ol.ProductId, ol.Quantity
FROM Orders o
JOIN OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderId = o.OrderId
WHERE o.SalesRepId = @RepId;
questions.modelAnswer:
A SELECT without an explicit hint doesn't normally take a table lock, so the first question is how that scan turned into one. With no supporting index on OrderLines for whatever predicate or join path the optimizer chose, the engine has to touch a large number of rows via a scan, taking a shared lock on each one it visits. SQL Server has a finite lock memory budget, and when the number of individual locks held by one statement crosses an internal threshold, it automatically escalates from many fine-grained row/page locks to a single table-level lock to reduce lock management overhead. That table-level shared lock is compatible with other readers but blocks writers outright, which is exactly why INSERTs into OrderLines pile up behind it even though the report is 'just reading.'

The fix starts with the execution plan: confirm there's a scan (not a seek) on OrderLines and identify which column the join or filter actually needs. If OrderLines has no index on OrderId (or on whatever column anchors the join to Orders), add a nonclustered index on that column, with included columns for ProductId and Quantity if this query is frequent enough to want a fully covering index. A seek against that index touches far fewer rows, likely staying well under the escalation threshold. If the table is simply very large and even a seek'ed range returns many rows, enabling Read Committed Snapshot Isolation removes the shared-lock-vs-insert conflict entirely for this pattern, since readers would work off row versions rather than blocking locks - though that's an instance-wide (or database-wide) behavior change that needs sign-off, not a drive-by fix. I'd pair the index fix with monitoring for LOCK_ESCALATION events going forward so this class of problem surfaces before users notice it again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by not trusting 'nothing changed in the code' as proof nothing changed - data volume grows even when queries don't, and a join that used to be cheap can quietly cross the row-count threshold where the optimizer stops seeking and starts scanning. So first I pull the actual execution plan for that report query and check OrderLines for a scan versus a seek. If it's scanning, that tells me there's no supporting index for the join, and all those row locks it's picking up along the way are what's triggering SQL Server's automatic lock escalation to a table lock - which is the real reason a read is blocking writes so hard. My fix is almost always to add the missing index first, because a seek that only touches the rows it needs rarely escalates at all. If I add the index and it's still escalating because the table's genuinely huge and the result set is wide, then I'd bring RCSI into the conversation as a bigger architectural change, but I wouldn't reach for that first since it changes isolation behavior for everyone, not just this one report.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderLines_OrderId ON dbo.OrderLines (OrderId) INCLUDE (ProductId, Quantity);
-- Verify with: SET STATISTICS IO ON; and re-check the plan for an Index Seek instead of a Clustered Index Scan on OrderLines.
commonMistakes: Assuming a SELECT can't cause serious blocking, so looking everywhere except the report query itself
Jumping straight to NOLOCK hints or snapshot isolation without first checking whether a missing index is the real root cause
Not checking sys.dm_tran_locks or the execution plan to confirm an escalation actually happened versus assuming it from symptoms alone
Adding an index without included columns, fixing the seek but still causing extra key lookups under load
Treating the fix as done without monitoring for future LOCK_ESCALATION events as data grows
keyPoints: Lock escalation automatically converts many row/page locks into one table lock once a statement exceeds the lock count threshold
A missing index forcing a scan is the most common trigger for escalation on an otherwise 'simple' read
Confirm with the execution plan (scan vs seek) and sys.dm_tran_locks before proposing a fix
A targeted covering index is usually the right first fix; RCSI is a bigger, instance-level decision
Index design should include the columns actually returned, not just the join key, to avoid extra lookups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the scan-to-lock-escalation mechanism
Identifies missing index as the likely root cause and how to confirm it
Proposes a correct, appropriately scoped index fix
Mentions RCSI as a secondary option with its tradeoffs, not a first resort
Clarity and structure of the answer

questions.title: A Pipeline That Fails on Two Nights Out of Seven, With No Retry Policy
questions.prompt: A nightly Data Factory pipeline copies data from an on-premises SQL Server to Azure Data Lake using a self-hosted integration runtime. It fails roughly two nights out of seven with a generic 'ErrorCode=SqlOperationFailed, Code=121, Timeout expired' message. There is no retry policy configured on the Copy activity. A manual rerun the next morning always succeeds. Describe how you'd investigate this and what you'd fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A generic SQL timeout on an intermittent schedule points me toward resource contention or network conditions rather than a logic bug, since the same pipeline and query succeed cleanly most nights and always on manual rerun. I'd start in the Monitor hub to confirm exactly which activity failed and its duration right up to the timeout, then check the self-hosted integration runtime's node health (CPU, memory, available connections) around the failure window, since a single-node self-hosted IR is a shared resource that can be starved by other on-premises activity - most commonly overlapping backup jobs, index maintenance windows, or other batch processes that happen to run at a similar time but not every night. I'd also check whether the source query itself does a large, unfiltered scan that depends on how much data has accumulated, since a slow night might simply be a night where the extract had more rows to move or the source server was mid-maintenance.

Once I understand the pattern, I'd apply two layers of fix. First, a basic safety net: add a retry policy on the Copy activity with a sensible interval and increase the command timeout, since 'fails twice a week, succeeds on manual rerun' is exactly the signature a modest retry policy is meant to catch automatically instead of requiring someone to notice and intervene by morning. Second, the actual root-cause fix: if it's resource contention from a single self-hosted IR node, I'd look at scaling to a second node for high availability and load distribution, or rescheduling the pipeline to avoid the overlapping on-prem maintenance window entirely. I'd also set up alerting on pipeline failure so this gets caught the same night rather than discovered by a user the next day, and log activity-level metrics to Log Analytics so the next intermittent issue has a historical pattern to compare against immediately.
questions.professionalAnswer: Intermittent plus 'works fine on manual rerun' is basically the classic signature of a resource or environment problem, not a code problem, so I wouldn't spend much time re-reading the pipeline logic itself. I'd go straight to the Monitor hub to nail down exactly which activity and how long it ran before timing out, and then I'd check the self-hosted IR's node health for those specific nights - CPU, memory, whatever else was running on that box around the same time. In my experience it's almost always something else on-prem competing for resources, like a backup window that doesn't run every single night. While I'm there I'd also just add a retry policy on the Copy activity, because honestly there's no excuse for not having one on an unattended nightly job - that alone would probably make this stop being a human-noticed problem even before I find the deeper cause. Longer term, if it really is IR resource contention, I'd push for a second IR node for redundancy and look at shifting the schedule a bit so it's not fighting with whatever else is hogging that server.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's a pipeline logic bug and re-reviewing the Copy activity configuration instead of checking IR and source-server resource health
Not adding a retry policy as a basic safety net, leaving an unattended nightly job with zero resilience to transient failures
Not checking for concurrent on-premises jobs (backups, maintenance) that could explain the intermittent pattern
Treating 'manual rerun works' as proof the problem is solved rather than evidence pointing toward a timing/resource issue
Not considering single self-hosted IR node as a single point of failure/bottleneck
keyPoints: Intermittent failure plus successful manual rerun points to resource contention or timing, not pipeline logic
Check self-hosted IR node health and concurrent on-premises jobs around the failure window
Add a retry policy and increase command timeout as an immediate safety net
Consider scaling the self-hosted IR to multiple nodes for both capacity and high availability
Set up alerting and centralized logging so intermittent issues are caught the same night

Describes concrete diagnostic steps (Monitor hub, IR node health, concurrent jobs)
Proposes retry policy and timeout tuning as immediate mitigation
Proposes IR scaling/HA or scheduling fix as the deeper remedy

questions.title: Terraform Apply Fails With 'Resource Already Exists' After a Manual Incident Fix
questions.prompt: During an incident last week, an engineer manually created a storage account and a couple of firewall rules directly in the Azure Portal to restore service quickly, without updating the Terraform code or state for the shared data-platform environment. Nobody has touched the Terraform configuration for those resources since. Today's terraform apply for that environment fails with Azure errors that the storage account and firewall rules already exist. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and safely bring Terraform back in sync, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the actual error carefully first: an Azure 'already exists' or conflict error on an apply, for a resource that terraform plan showed as 'will be created' rather than 'will be updated,' is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change -- the real resource exists in Azure, but Terraform's state has no record of it, so Terraform tries to create it from scratch and Azure's own uniqueness constraints reject the duplicate.

I'd confirm the drift explicitly rather than assume it: run terraform plan and verify the affected resources show as '+ create,' and cross-reference the resource names/IDs from the error against what's actually visible via az resource show or the Portal. In this case that directly confirms the incident-week manual resources are the cause.

Structurally, this happens because Terraform state is only ever updated by Terraform itself -- through apply, import, or refresh. Any resource created directly through the Portal, the CLI, or by an engineer bypassing Terraform is completely invisible to the state file no matter how long it's existed, and a plan has no way to discover it on its own; it only compares the configuration against what's already recorded in state.

The fix is terraform import. For each drifted resource, I'd get its real Azure resource ID (az resource show --name ... --resource-group ... --resource-type ... --query id) and run terraform import <resource_address_in_config> <azure_resource_id> to attach the real object into state under the matching address. This requires a resource block already existing in the .tf configuration for that address -- import only binds state, it doesn't generate configuration, unless using Terraform's newer import block with -generate-config-out, which can scaffold a starting config from the real resource if the .tf code doesn't exist yet.

After importing, I'd immediately run terraform plan again -- this is the step people skip. Import only syncs the state's existence record; it says nothing about whether the .tf configuration's attributes actually match what was configured manually during the incident (for example, a firewall rule's IP range might differ from what's in code). The follow-up plan will show any genuine attribute drift as an '~ update,' which has to be reconciled deliberately: either update the .tf code to match the real, intentional incident configuration, or apply to bring the resource back to the originally-intended configuration, depending on which is actually correct going forward.

Beyond the immediate fix, I'd treat this as a process signal: if manual changes during an incident are sometimes unavoidable, build a habit or runbook step of importing them back into Terraform (or at minimum filing a ticket to do so) right after the incident closes, rather than discovering the drift weeks later at the next unrelated apply.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The error message itself tells me almost everything before I look at anything else -- Azure saying a resource 'already exists' on something Terraform's plan wanted to create, not update, is basically the textbook signature of state drift. Something real exists out there that Terraform's state file has simply never heard of.

I wouldn't just assume that, though -- I'd run plan and actually look at whether it's showing a '+ create' for those resources, and cross-check the names against what's genuinely sitting in the Portal or az resource show. In this case that's trivial to confirm, because we already know exactly what happened: someone created these by hand in the Portal during last week's incident, and nothing about that touched Terraform's code or state.

The mechanical reason this happens is worth being precise about: Terraform's state file only ever gets updated by Terraform itself. It has no way to notice, on its own, that a human created something matching its configuration out-of-band -- it just compares its config against whatever it already has on record, and if there's no record, its only option is to try to create it, which collides with the real one that's already there.

So the fix is terraform import -- get the real Azure resource ID, point it at the matching resource address in the .tf config, and import binds the two together in state. The part I'd be careful not to skip is what comes right after: import only fixes the fact that Terraform now knows the resource exists. It says nothing about whether the configuration in code actually matches what got configured by hand during the incident. So the very next thing is another plan, and whatever shows up as an update this time -- maybe a firewall rule's IP range doesn't match -- is a deliberate decision to make: update the code to reflect the real, intentional incident fix, or apply to bring it back to what was originally intended. Either is fine, but it has to be a decision, not an accident. And longer-term, I'd push for a habit of importing incident-time manual changes back into Terraform right away, rather than discovering this kind of drift at the next unrelated apply weeks later.
questions.example:
# Get the real Azure resource ID
az storage account show --name stdataplat01 --resource-group rg-data-platform --query id -o tsv

# Bind it into state at the matching config address
terraform import azurerm_storage_account.data_platform \
  /subscriptions/xxxx/resourceGroups/rg-data-platform/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stdataplat01

# ALWAYS re-plan after import to catch attribute-level drift
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Assuming the Terraform code itself is broken since 'nothing in it changed'
Deleting the manually-created Azure resources to let Terraform recreate them cleanly, discarding the incident fix
Running terraform import without first confirming via plan which specific resources/attributes are actually drifted
Treating import as a complete fix and not re-running plan afterward to catch attribute-level drift
Importing into the wrong resource address, not matching an existing/correct resource block, causing a different drift
keyPoints: 'Already exists' on a planned create, not an update, is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change
Terraform state only changes via Terraform itself; manually-created resources are invisible to it until explicitly imported
terraform import attaches an existing real resource to a state address but requires a matching config block (or the import block with -generate-config-out)
Import only fixes existence tracking -- a follow-up plan is required to catch and reconcile attribute-level drift
Process takeaway: import out-of-band incident changes back into Terraform promptly, not weeks later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses 'already exists on a create' as state drift from an out-of-band manual change
Explains why Terraform state doesn't auto-discover manually created resources
Walks through terraform import correctly (resource ID lookup, address, requires config)
Emphasizes re-running plan after import to catch attribute drift
Notes a process improvement for future incidents

questions.title: A Stuck Terraform State Lock Is Blocking Every Deployment After a CI Crash
questions.prompt: A CI pipeline running terraform apply against a remote state backend lost network connectivity partway through and the job was killed before it could finish. Every terraform apply, and even terraform plan, run against that environment since has failed immediately with a state lock error, and the team is blocked from deploying anything to that environment. Walk through how you'd safely diagnose and resolve this, in the order you'd actually do it, including what you'd check before touching the lock.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the lock error output carefully first. Most backends that support locking (Azure Storage via a blob lease, S3 with a DynamoDB lock table, Terraform Cloud) surface identifying details directly in the error -- a Lock ID, who or what acquired it, and a timestamp. That information is the starting point, not something to skip past to get straight to unlocking.

Before touching anything, I'd rule out that this is a real, currently-in-progress apply rather than a stale lock left behind by the crashed job. I'd check the CI system's own run history or dashboard for that environment to confirm no other pipeline run is actively executing right now, and if there's any ambiguity I'd check with the team or on-call directly. The entire point of the lock is to prevent two concurrent applies from reading and writing the shared state file at the same time, which can corrupt it -- one apply's changes getting silently overwritten by the other's stale read is the real danger here, not a hypothetical one, so removing a lock that's protecting a genuinely active apply is the actual risk I'm managing against.

Once I've confirmed no other apply is running, I'd check whether the underlying state storage itself was left in a bad condition by the crash, not just locked -- for an Azure Storage backend, checking the blob's lease status directly (az storage blob show), and checking whether blob soft-delete or versioning is enabled so I could inspect or recover a prior good version of the state file if needed. For other backends I'd check the equivalent, such as a DynamoDB lock table item for S3, or the run status in Terraform Cloud.

To resolve the stale lock itself, I'd run terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> using the Lock ID from the error message. This only removes the lock record; it doesn't touch or validate the actual state file contents.

Immediately afterward I'd verify state integrity before trusting it: run terraform plan and read it carefully. If the crashed apply got partway through actually changing real infrastructure before losing connectivity, the state file may not fully reflect that, and the plan might show unexpected diffs for resources that were mid-change. I'd compare anything surprising against what's actually deployed (az resource show or the Portal) before applying further, and if the state looks meaningfully inconsistent with reality, I'd consider reconciling it or, in the worst case, pulling a previous good state version from backend versioning rather than trusting a possibly-partial write.

Once plan looks sane, I'd proceed with a normal apply. As a process follow-up, I'd flag whether the CI pipeline needs better handling for interrupted runs -- a cleanup step, or relying on the backend's native lease/lock timeout where supported -- so an infrastructure blip doesn't require a manual force-unlock every time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I touch the lock at all, I want to understand what it's actually there to prevent, because that framing changes how carefully I approach this. The lock exists so two applies can't read and write the same state file at the same time -- if that happened, one apply's changes could silently get clobbered by the other's stale read, which is a much worse problem than being temporarily blocked. So my first move isn't force-unlock, it's making sure I'm not about to remove a lock that's protecting something that's genuinely still running.

I'd check the CI system's own history for that environment to confirm nothing is actively executing, and if there's any doubt, I'd just ask the team directly rather than guess. Once I'm confident the lock is stale -- left behind by the job that got killed mid-run when it lost connectivity -- I'd look at the lock error itself, which for most backends gives me a Lock ID and some context about who/what acquired it, and I'd also check the underlying storage directly, like the blob's lease status if this is an Azure Storage backend, to see if there's anything else inconsistent beyond just the lock.

Then force-unlock with that specific Lock ID. But I don't treat that as the finish line -- force-unlock only removes the lock record, it doesn't tell me anything about whether the state file itself is trustworthy after a crash that happened mid-apply. So the very next thing is a plan, read carefully: if the crashed run had actually started changing real infrastructure before it lost connectivity, the state might not fully reflect that, and I'd expect to see it in unexpected diffs. If anything looks off, I'd rather pull a known-good prior version of the state from the backend's versioning than apply on top of something I don't trust. Only once plan looks sane do I let anyone apply again, and I'd flag the CI pipeline's handling of interrupted runs as a real follow-up so this doesn't become a recurring manual fire drill.
questions.example:
# Error typically includes the Lock ID and holder info:
# Error: Error acquiring the state lock
# Lock Info:
#   ID:        7f3a1c2e-...
#   Operation: OperationTypeApply
#   Who:       ci-runner-42
#   Created:   2026-10-02 09:14:03 UTC

# Confirm no apply is genuinely still running (CI history), then:
az storage blob show --container-name tfstate --name prod.terraform.tfstate --account-name tfstateacct

terraform force-unlock 7f3a1c2e-...

# Verify state integrity before trusting it
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Running terraform force-unlock immediately without first confirming no apply is genuinely still in progress
Treating the lock itself as the problem rather than asking what it's protecting against
Assuming the state file is definitely fine once the lock is removed, without reviewing plan output for signs of a partial write
Not checking whether the crashed apply actually changed real infrastructure before the connection dropped
Manually deleting the lock blob/file instead of using the proper force-unlock command, risking an inconsistent backend locking state
keyPoints: The lock exists to prevent two concurrent applies from corrupting shared state via simultaneous read-modify-write, not as an arbitrary safeguard
Always confirm no apply is genuinely still running before force-unlocking
terraform force-unlock removes the lock record only; it doesn't validate or repair the state file itself
Review plan output carefully afterward for signs the crashed apply partially changed infrastructure
Backend versioning/soft-delete, where available, is the safety net if the state file itself looks inconsistent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains what the lock actually protects against
Confirms no concurrent apply is running before acting
Correctly uses terraform force-unlock with the Lock ID
Verifies state/plan integrity after unlocking rather than assuming it's fine
Notes a process improvement or backend-recovery safety net

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);

Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

questions.title: Designing Secure Credential Management After a Data Factory Security Audit
questions.prompt: A security audit of your Data Factory environment found linked services with embedded SQL authentication connection strings, including a hardcoded password on one, and a service principal holding Owner on the entire subscription used for Blob Storage access. Design the correct credential and access architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the hardcoded SQL password, the fix is to move it into Azure Key Vault and have the linked service reference it through Key Vault integration rather than storing it in plaintext in the pipeline definition or in any ARM template - that alone makes the credential centrally managed, rotatable, and no longer visible anywhere in source control or deployment artifacts. For the Blob Storage access using an Owner-scoped service principal, I'd go further than just better-hiding that credential: I'd replace it entirely with Data Factory's system-assigned (or user-assigned) managed identity, which removes the need to store or rotate a credential for that connection at all, since Azure handles the identity's authentication behind the scenes.

Whichever identity or service principal remains in use, I'd scope its RBAC role down to exactly what it needs at the narrowest resource boundary that works - Storage Blob Data Contributor on the specific storage account or container it actually touches, never Owner at the subscription level, which is wildly disproportionate to what a pipeline's data-movement activity actually requires. For SQL access specifically, I'd prefer Azure AD authentication via the managed identity where the target is Azure SQL, or if the source is on-premises SQL Server, I'd make sure the self-hosted integration runtime's own service account is tightly scoped and that whatever credential remains in Key Vault has a defined rotation and expiry policy rather than being set-and-forgotten. I'd close this out by removing the subscription-level Owner service principal entirely once the replacement access is validated, adding diagnostic logging and alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes to catch future drift, and scheduling a recurring (e.g., quarterly) access review so this becomes an ongoing control rather than a one-time cleanup following an audit finding.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the hardcoded password, that's the easy part to fix - move it into Key Vault and have the linked service pull it from there, so it's never sitting in plaintext in a pipeline definition or an ARM template again. The Owner-on-the-whole-subscription service principal is the part I'd actually spend more time on, because just hiding that credential better in Key Vault doesn't fix the underlying problem - the access itself is wildly overscoped. I'd replace it with Data Factory's managed identity wherever possible, so there's no stored credential at all for that connection, and then scope whatever RBAC role it actually needs down to the specific storage account, not the entire subscription. For SQL, I'd lean on Azure AD authentication through that same managed identity if it's Azure SQL, and if it's still on-prem, I'd make sure the self-hosted IR's service account and whatever's left in Key Vault has an actual rotation schedule instead of being set once and forgotten. And I wouldn't call this done after one cleanup pass - I'd want diagnostic alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes, plus a recurring access review, so this doesn't quietly drift back to where it started.
commonMistakes: Moving the password into Key Vault without also addressing the separately serious issue of subscription-level Owner scope
Not considering managed identity as a way to eliminate stored credentials entirely rather than just hiding them better
Granting a 'safer-sounding' but still overly broad role instead of the specific minimal RBAC role actually needed
Not planning credential rotation or an ongoing access review, treating this as a one-time cleanup
Not addressing authentication specifically for the on-premises SQL Server side
keyPoints: Key Vault-backed linked services eliminate plaintext/embedded credentials
Managed identity eliminates stored credentials for Blob Storage access entirely where supported
Scope RBAC to least privilege at the specific resource level, never subscription-level Owner
Prefer Azure AD authentication for SQL where possible
Establish ongoing credential rotation and periodic access review, not a one-time fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes Key Vault integration for remaining credentials
Proposes managed identity to eliminate stored credentials where possible
Correctly scopes RBAC to least privilege
Addresses ongoing rotation/review process
Clarity

questions.title: Designing Remote State Architecture for a Three-Environment Azure Data Platform
questions.prompt: You're moving a Terraform-managed Azure data platform from one engineer's local state file to a proper dev/staging/prod setup. Design the remote state architecture: how many state files, how they're isolated from each other, how locking works, and how a change gets promoted from dev to prod without anyone ever being able to accidentally run apply against the wrong environment.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core decision is separate state files (and ideally separate backend storage) per environment, rather than one state file with Terraform workspaces. Workspaces are attractive because they let the same backend config serve multiple named states, but they typically share the same backend credentials and often the same service principal, which means a mistake (wrong workspace selected, a bad variable) can still reach another environment's state. Separate backends — a storage account/container/key path per environment, e.g. key = "dev.terraform.tfstate" vs "prod.terraform.tfstate", ideally in resource groups or even subscriptions scoped per environment — give real isolation: a dev-scoped service principal literally cannot authenticate against the prod backend or prod Azure subscription, so there's no 'accidentally' about it.

Locking is handled natively by the azurerm backend via blob lease (an ETag-based optimistic lock on the state blob), so no separate lock table is needed the way some other backends require. For promotion: the same Terraform module code is reused across environments, with environment-specific values supplied via separate .tfvars files (dev.tfvars, prod.tfvars) — never separate copies of the module logic itself, which would drift. The actual apply never happens from an engineer's laptop; a CI pipeline runs terraform plan on every PR against the target environment's backend, and a prod apply requires a manual approval gate after the plan is reviewed, using a prod-scoped service principal with least-privilege RBAC that the pipeline injects, which an engineer's local machine never has credentials for at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd give each environment its own state file in its own backend path — dev, staging, prod each with their own key in the storage account, ideally scoped to different resource groups so the blast radius of a mistake in one environment can't physically touch another. I'd lean away from using Terraform workspaces as the only isolation here, because workspaces usually share the same backend credentials, and I want it to be structurally impossible for a dev credential to touch prod, not just procedurally discouraged.

Locking comes for free with the azurerm backend — it uses a blob lease, so two applies against the same state just serialize instead of racing. For promotion, it's the same module code everywhere with a different .tfvars file per environment — never copy-pasted module logic, because that drifts fast. And nobody runs apply locally against prod at all — that only happens through a pipeline, which plans on every PR, and prod specifically needs a human to approve the plan before it applies, using credentials scoped to prod that are only available inside that pipeline run.
commonMistakes: Using Terraform workspaces as the only environment isolation when distinct access control per environment is actually needed
Keeping all environments in a single state file or a single backend path
Allowing engineers to run apply locally against any environment, especially prod
Copy-pasting module logic per environment instead of reusing one module with per-environment .tfvars
Not scoping service principal credentials per environment, so a dev identity can technically reach prod
keyPoints: Separate state files/backends per environment give real isolation, not just naming convention
Workspaces share backend credentials and are weaker isolation than separate backends for this use case
The azurerm backend provides native locking via blob lease, no separate lock table needed
Promotion reuses the same module code with environment-specific .tfvars, never duplicated logic
Prod applies run only through CI with a manual approval gate and prod-scoped credentials never available locally

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recommends separate state/backends per environment with reasoning
Correctly addresses locking mechanism
Describes a concrete promotion flow using shared code + environment-specific variables
Describes how accidental wrong-environment applies are structurally prevented, not just discouraged

questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.
questions.example: Split: (1) Validate CLV calculation logic with Product, (2) Confirm/connect data sources, (3) Build semantic model & measures, (4) Build dashboard visualization — each separately estimated.
commonMistakes: Accepting a vague, oversized story as a single sprint item without decomposing it
Silently re-estimating the story unilaterally instead of involving the team
Publicly undermining the junior analyst's original estimate instead of framing it as a normal grooming gap
Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery
keyPoints: Decomposes a vague, oversized backlog item into independently valuable, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation and data-source unknowns during grooming, not mid-sprint
Reframes the original estimate's gap constructively rather than as a mistake by the junior analyst
Facilitates collaborative team re-estimation rather than overriding unilaterally
Models proactive unknown-surfacing as a senior responsibility within the Scrum process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and decomposes the oversized/ambiguous story into discrete, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation logic and data source unknowns proactively during grooming
Handles the junior analyst's original estimate constructively and respectfully
Uses collaborative, team-based re-estimation rather than unilateral override
Demonstrates understanding of how senior ownership operates within the Scrum process

questions.title: Moving a Portal-Clicking Team to Terraform/Bicep Over Skeptical Senior Pushback
questions.prompt: Your team has always provisioned Azure resources by clicking through the portal, and you want to move the team to Terraform/Bicep for a new data platform build. Two senior teammates are skeptical, citing 'it's slower than just clicking the thing I need' and past frustration with a previous team's over-engineered Terraform setup. How do you negotiate this adoption?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the skepticism as legitimate signal rather than resistance to be overcome by mandate. The candidate should start by separating the two objections, since they need different responses: 'portal is faster for a one-off' is often true and should be acknowledged honestly rather than argued away, while the past bad experience with over-engineered Terraform is a real scar that a new rollout needs to explicitly design against -- by keeping the initial module set small, flat, and genuinely necessary rather than building abstraction layers nobody asked for.

The candidate should propose an approach that lets the skeptics experience the value rather than being told about it: start with a new, lower-stakes piece of the platform build, let the team keep clicking for genuinely one-off exploratory resources for now, and bring the skeptics into writing the first modules rather than handing them a framework decided in isolation. The real argument for adoption -- consistent, reviewable, repeatable environments; drift detection; faster disaster recovery -- should be made concretely against this specific platform build's needs, not as an abstract best-practice argument, and the candidate should be honest that there's a real short-term velocity cost that pays off over the project's lifetime, not instantly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win an argument -- I'd go in treating their pushback as two separate, legitimate points that need different answers. 'Clicking is faster for the thing I need right now' is just true a lot of the time, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 'the last Terraform setup I used was over-engineered and painful' is the one I actually need to address head-on, by being explicit that whatever we build this time starts small and flat -- no module-of-modules, no abstraction for things we don't have yet.

Practically, I'd rather let them feel the benefit than argue them into it. I'd pick a lower-stakes piece of the new platform build to go first, keep it genuinely simple, and actually have the two of them help write those first modules instead of handing them something I designed alone and asking them to adopt it. And I'd be straight with them that yes, this is going to be a bit slower than clicking for the first few weeks -- the payoff is in repeatable environments and not having to remember what we clicked six months from now when we need to rebuild something, and that's a real tradeoff, not a free win I'm selling them.
commonMistakes: Treating the skepticism as pure resistance to change instead of partially valid feedback
Arguing that Terraform is strictly faster, which isn't true for small one-off changes and damages credibility
Ignoring or dismissing the team's past bad experience with an over-engineered IaC setup instead of designing against it
Mandating the switch top-down without letting the skeptics co-author the first real modules
Overselling adoption as a free win instead of being honest about the short-term velocity cost
keyPoints: Separates the 'portal is faster' objection from the 'past over-engineering' objection and addresses each specifically
Explicitly designs the new rollout to be small and simple, directly countering the past bad experience
Lets skeptics experience the value on a real, lower-stakes piece of work rather than mandating from above
Involves the skeptical senior teammates in authoring the first modules
Is honest about the real short-term velocity tradeoff rather than overselling adoption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates and responds to the two distinct objections
Proposes a concrete plan to avoid repeating the past over-engineering experience
Involves the skeptical teammates directly rather than mandating adoption top-down
Makes a concrete, project-specific case for adoption rather than an abstract best-practices argument
Is honest about real tradeoffs instead of overselling the change

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on a Terraform Apply That Took Down a Shared Event Hub
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` run by a teammate, approved in a rushed review, took down a shared production Event Hub namespace for 40 minutes before anyone noticed. You're leading the blameless postmortem. How do you run it so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless does not mean avoiding naming what happened -- the postmortem should state plainly that a specific Terraform change, approved in a rushed review, triggered the outage, while keeping the framing on the system that allowed it rather than on the individuals as people. The candidate should reframe the central question from 'who broke the Event Hub' to 'what let a plan with this blast radius get approved in a rushed review, and why did it take 40 minutes to notice a shared production namespace was down.' That reframing is what produces durable fixes instead of two people -- the author and the reviewer -- feeling punished while the same gap exists for the next risky change.

The candidate should explicitly involve both the author and the reviewer in walking through their reasoning: what the plan output looked like, what time pressure existed, why the blast radius of the change (a shared resource used by other teams) wasn't flagged in review. The postmortem should close with concrete, owned, dated action items distinct from the individuals' behavior -- for example, requiring plan output to explicitly call out changes to shared/cross-team resources, a mandatory second reviewer or cooling-off period for changes touching shared infrastructure, and alerting on the Event Hub namespace's health so a future outage is caught in minutes, not 40.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we're vague about what happened -- I'll say directly that a specific apply, approved in a review that got rushed, is what took the namespace down. But I keep steering the room toward the system question: what let a change with this big a blast radius get approved quickly, and why did it take 40 minutes before anyone noticed a shared production resource was gone, rather than who personally messed up.

I'd ask both the person who wrote the change and the person who reviewed it to actually walk through their side -- what the plan output showed, what the time pressure looked like, whether anything flagged that this touched a resource other teams depend on. And I'm not going to let the meeting end as just a good conversation -- I want it to end with specific fixes: plan output that calls out changes to shared resources explicitly, maybe a required second reviewer or a short cooling-off window for anything touching shared infra, and health alerting on that namespace so next time we catch it in minutes instead of 40.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'blameless' with being vague about what actually happened or who was involved
Focusing on the individual author's or reviewer's judgment instead of the systemic review gap
Not inviting both the author and the reviewer to explain their actual context and reasoning
Treating the 40-minute detection delay as a footnote instead of an equally important separate finding
Ending with a narrative discussion but no concrete, owned, dated action items
keyPoints: States plainly what happened and who was involved without making it about individual blame
Reframes toward the systemic gap: why a high-blast-radius change cleared a rushed review
Involves both the author and reviewer constructively to surface real context
Treats the 40-minute detection delay as its own distinct, important finding
Closes with concrete, owned, dated action items covering both the review gap and detection gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes blameless from avoiding naming the actual cause and people involved
Reframes the discussion toward the systemic review gap rather than individual fault
Involves both author and reviewer constructively to surface context, not blame
Identifies the detection delay as a separate, equally important finding
Produces concrete, owned, dated action items addressing both gaps

questions.title: Taking Ownership of a Terraform-Managed Platform With Months of Undocumented Manual Drift
questions.prompt: You've just become the owner of a Terraform-managed Azure data platform. The previous owner left, and terraform plan against the current code shows dozens of unexpected changes — resources that were modified directly in the portal during past incidents and never reconciled back into the .tf files. How do you take this over responsibly, and in what order do you act?
questions.modelAnswer:
The first instinct to resist is running terraform apply to 'clean up' the drift immediately — that would blindly revert every manually-made change back to whatever the code says, including emergency fixes that were made during real incidents and may still be the correct state today. The responsible first step is going through the plan output resource by resource and classifying each drifted item as either (a) an intentional fix that should be promoted into the code, meaning the .tf is updated to match what's actually running, or (b) genuine accidental drift that should be reverted to match the declared config. That classification work requires cross-referencing incident tickets/history and talking to whoever on the team remembers the context, not just reading the diff in isolation.

Only after the code has been reconciled to reflect the intentionally-kept changes should any apply run — and that apply should happen in a low-traffic window with a clear rollback plan, ideally validated against a non-prod environment first if one exists. Alongside the reconciliation itself, a strong answer flags the actual process gap: there was no mechanism catching this drift as it accumulated over months, so proposing a recurring drift-detection job (a scheduled terraform plan in CI, alerting on any nonzero diff) is part of taking real ownership, not just the one-time cleanup. The tone throughout should be about fixing the gap, not assigning blame to the person who left for making emergency fixes under pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I would absolutely not do first is just run apply to force everything back to what the code says — some of those manual changes were probably the actual fix for a real incident, and blindly reverting them could reintroduce the exact problem someone fixed under pressure. So step one is going through the plan diff item by item and figuring out, for each one, whether it's a change that should be written back into the code because it's the right state, or something that genuinely drifted and should be reverted. That means digging through incident history and talking to whoever's still around, not just eyeballing the diff.

Once the code actually reflects what should be true, that's when I'd run an apply — and I'd do it in a quiet window with a rollback plan ready, not casually. And I'd use this as the moment to fix the actual gap, which is that nothing caught this drift accumulating for months in the first place — so I'd set up a scheduled plan in CI that alerts the moment there's any drift, so I'm never discovering six months of undocumented changes again. And I'd try not to make this about the previous owner having done something wrong under incident pressure — that's just what happens without a drift-detection process, and now it's mine to fix.
commonMistakes: Running terraform apply immediately to 'clean up' drift without first understanding why each change was made
Treating every drifted resource identically instead of classifying each one as intentional-fix vs. accidental
Blaming the previous owner instead of focusing on reconciliation and the missing process
Reconciling the drift once but not setting up any ongoing drift detection, so the problem recurs
Applying the reconciliation directly against prod without a low-traffic window or rollback plan
keyPoints: Never blindly apply to force drift back to code before understanding what each change was for
Classify each drifted resource individually as 'promote into code' vs. 'revert to code', using incident history
Apply the reconciled config carefully — low-traffic window, rollback plan, non-prod validation if possible
Propose ongoing drift detection (scheduled plan in CI with alerting) to prevent recurrence
Frames the response around fixing the process gap, not blaming the predecessor

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explicitly avoids blindly applying to revert drift without investigation
Describes a concrete per-resource reconciliation approach using incident context
Describes a careful, safe apply process once reconciled
Proposes ongoing drift detection to prevent recurrence

questions.title: DTU, vCore, and Hyperscale: What Each Model Actually Charges You For
questions.prompt: Explain, at the mechanical level, what you are actually paying for under the DTU purchasing model versus the vCore model for Azure SQL Database, and what makes the Hyperscale service tier architecturally different from either of them rather than just 'vCore with a bigger ceiling.' A client currently on a DTU S3 tier is seeing CPU pegged at 100% while storage and I/O are nowhere near their limits — what does that tell you, and what would you move them to?
questions.modelAnswer:
The DTU (Database Transaction Unit) model bundles CPU, memory, and I/O into a single blended unit — when Microsoft says 'S3 has 100 DTUs,' that number represents a fixed ratio of those three resources measured against a benchmark workload, and you cannot independently scale one dimension. If your workload's actual bottleneck is CPU but your DTU tier's blend over-provisions I/O relative to what you need, you're paying for I/O capacity you can't use while still being capped on CPU — you have no way to buy 'more CPU, same I/O' under DTU. The vCore model unbundles this: you choose a number of virtual cores and an amount of memory somewhat independently (within each service tier's allowed combinations), and you can also choose compute and storage separately, including choosing your own Azure Hybrid Benefit-eligible licensing. This directly exposes which resource is actually the bottleneck and lets you pay for more of only that resource.

Hyperscale is not simply 'vCore turned up.' It's a different storage architecture entirely: instead of a single attached disk capped at a few terabytes with the compute node, Hyperscale decouples storage into a distributed, log-structured architecture across multiple page server replicas, with near-instant backups implemented as storage snapshots (not a multi-hour COPY_ONLY backup job) and fast restores regardless of database size, plus the ability to scale storage to many terabytes without the downtime a storage resize normally requires on General Purpose/Business Critical. It also supports rapid compute rescale and additional read-scale replicas beyond what Business Critical's HA replicas offer. The key distinction for an interview: General Purpose and Business Critical scale storage and compute together on the same node up to a hard ceiling; Hyperscale scales storage independently and nearly unboundedly, which is the actual architectural difference, not just 'a bigger number.'

For the specific symptom — CPU pegged at 100% while storage/IO are well under their limits on DTU S3 — that's a textbook signal of a resource-blend mismatch, not a true capacity problem. The workload needs more compute specifically, not more of the bundled I/O/storage DTU S3 also includes. I'd move them to vCore General Purpose (or Business Critical if they also need higher availability/lower-latency storage) and size the vCores based on observed CPU utilization at the current workload, rather than jumping tiers within DTU, which would scale all three resources together and over-provision I/O/storage they don't need just to get more CPU.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always explain DTU as a bundle deal — you're buying a fixed ratio of CPU, memory, and I/O all glued together, and you can't change that ratio, only the overall size of the bundle. So if your workload's bottleneck doesn't match that ratio — which is exactly what's happening with this S3 database pegged on CPU but fine on storage and I/O — you're stuck either staying capped on CPU or buying a bigger bundle that also gives you a bunch of I/O and storage headroom you were never going to use. vCore fixes that by letting you choose compute and storage as separate dials, so you can specifically add CPU without dragging unneeded I/O capacity along with it, and it also opens the door to licensing savings through Azure Hybrid Benefit if they already own SQL Server licenses.

Hyperscale I always flag as a different conversation entirely, because people assume it's just 'vCore but bigger,' and that undersells what's actually going on. The storage layer is completely redesigned — it's distributed across page servers instead of living on one attached disk, which is why Hyperscale backups are basically instant snapshots instead of the long-running backup job you'd see on General Purpose, and why you can scale into many terabytes without the downtime a normal storage resize would force on you. That's a genuinely different architecture under the hood, not a bigger size slider.

For this specific client, I'd tell them plainly: your CPU is maxed and everything else has headroom, which means you're paying for I/O and storage you don't need just to unlock more CPU on the DTU ladder. Move to vCore General Purpose, size it to the CPU you're actually burning, and you'll likely end up paying for closer to what you actually use instead of a blended tier that was never shaped around your workload.
commonMistakes: Assuming Hyperscale is just a higher vCore tier rather than a different storage architecture
Scaling up within DTU tiers to fix a single-resource bottleneck, over-provisioning the other two resources
Not recognizing that vCore allows separating compute sizing from storage sizing
Forgetting Azure Hybrid Benefit only applies to vCore, not DTU
Ignoring that Hyperscale backup/restore speed is independent of database size, unlike General Purpose/Business Critical
keyPoints: DTU bundles CPU/memory/I/O into one fixed ratio you cannot scale independently
vCore unbundles compute and storage, and allows independent scaling plus Azure Hybrid Benefit licensing
Hyperscale uses a distributed, page-server storage architecture, not a bigger version of attached-disk storage
Hyperscale backups are near-instant snapshots and storage scales without the downtime a resize normally causes
A CPU-pegged, I/O-light workload signals a resource-blend mismatch, best solved by vCore sized to CPU need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the DTU bundled-resource model and its limitation
Correctly explains vCore's independent compute/storage scaling and licensing benefit
Correctly identifies Hyperscale's distributed storage architecture as the real differentiator
Correctly diagnoses the CPU-pegged scenario and recommends vCore sized to CPU
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: Always Encrypted vs. Always Encrypted with Secure Enclaves: What Changes Under the Hood
questions.prompt: Explain how standard Always Encrypted actually protects data end-to-end, including what the driver does and what SQL Server itself is never allowed to see. Then explain specifically what a secure enclave adds, what becomes possible with enclaves that is impossible with standard Always Encrypted, and the trade-off a DBA takes on by enabling enclave-based computations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Standard Always Encrypted keeps plaintext data out of SQL Server's reach entirely, by design: a column designated as encrypted is encrypted client-side, inside the application's ODBC/JDBC driver (or ADO.NET provider) using a column encryption key the driver fetches and unwraps via a column master key, which typically lives somewhere outside the database entirely — a certificate store or Azure Key Vault. SQL Server stores and returns only ciphertext; it never possesses the keys needed to decrypt, so even a DBA with sysadmin rights querying the table directly sees encrypted binary values, not plaintext. This is what people mean by 'the database engine never sees the plaintext.' The cost of this design is real functional limits: SQL Server can perform equality comparisons against deterministically-encrypted columns (so WHERE EncryptedColumn = @value works, because identical plaintexts always produce identical ciphertext under deterministic encryption), but it cannot do range comparisons, pattern matching (LIKE), computations, or most built-in functions against encrypted columns at all, because the engine has no way to operate on ciphertext meaningfully — any such operation would have to happen client-side after decryption.

A secure enclave changes this by giving SQL Server a hardware- or software-isolated, attested region of memory where it can decrypt data temporarily and perform richer computation — pattern matching, range comparisons, in-place cryptographic operations for initial encryption or key rotation — without that plaintext ever being visible outside the enclave, including to the SQL Server process itself running outside the enclave boundary, the OS, or an administrator inspecting memory. The enclave proves its own integrity to the client driver via attestation before the driver will release keys into it, so the client isn't just trusting SQL Server's word that it's using an enclave correctly. This is what makes operations like server-side LIKE queries or in-place encryption of existing plaintext columns (without exporting data to a client app first) possible with enclaves but categorically impossible with standard Always Encrypted.

The trade-off: enabling enclave computations means trusting the enclave technology itself (and its attestation service — typically Microsoft Azure Attestation for Azure SQL) as part of your security boundary, which is a broader attack surface than 'the server never has the keys at all.' It also has real operational cost — enclave-enabled columns typically require the newer 'randomized encryption with enclave computations' and specific driver/compatibility-level support, and attestation adds a dependency and a potential availability/latency factor that doesn't exist in the simpler, zero-trust-in-server model. A DBA choosing enclaves is deliberately trading a small amount of additional trusted surface area for meaningfully richer query capability against encrypted data.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd explain standard Always Encrypted is: the server is completely blind. Encryption and decryption happen in the client driver, the keys live outside SQL Server — often in Key Vault — and all SQL Server ever sees or stores is ciphertext. That's true even for me as a DBA with full admin rights; I can query the table directly and all I get back is encrypted bytes. The catch is that blindness has a cost — SQL Server can do an equality check against deterministically-encrypted data because identical plaintext always maps to identical ciphertext, but it can't do a range filter, a LIKE, or run any function against that column, because it genuinely cannot operate meaningfully on ciphertext it can't read.

A secure enclave is Microsoft's answer to that limitation — it's a protected, attested little sandbox inside the server where SQL Server actually can decrypt and compute on real data temporarily, without that plaintext ever leaking out to the rest of the SQL Server process, the OS, or anyone looking at memory from outside. The attestation piece matters a lot to me — the client driver doesn't just take SQL Server's word that there's a legitimate enclave running; it gets cryptographic proof from an attestation service before it'll even hand over the keys. That's what unlocks things that are flatly impossible otherwise, like running a LIKE against encrypted data server-side, or doing in-place encryption of a column that already has plaintext data in it without having to round-trip every row through a client app first.

The trade-off I'd be upfront about with a security team: you're adding a little bit of trusted surface area back in — you now have to trust the enclave hardware/software and the attestation service — in exchange for real query flexibility. It's not free, and there's real setup overhead around attestation and driver/compatibility requirements, but for a lot of real applications, giving up the absolute zero-trust-in-server guarantee for workable range queries and pattern matching is worth it.
commonMistakes: Believing a DBA with sysadmin rights can read Always Encrypted plaintext directly from the table
Assuming any WHERE clause works against an Always Encrypted column, not just deterministic equality
Thinking secure enclaves eliminate the need for column/master key management
Not understanding that attestation is what prevents a compromised server from faking enclave behavior
Treating enclave-based Always Encrypted as strictly more secure rather than a different trust trade-off
keyPoints: Standard Always Encrypted decrypts only in the client driver; SQL Server stores and sees only ciphertext
Deterministic encryption allows equality comparisons server-side; randomized encryption doesn't even allow that
Range queries, LIKE, and computations are impossible against standard Always Encrypted columns
Secure enclaves give SQL Server an attested, isolated region to decrypt and compute without exposing plaintext elsewhere
Attestation (e.g., Azure Attestation) proves enclave integrity to the client before keys are released
Enclaves trade a small increase in trusted surface area for richer server-side query capability

Correctly distinguishes deterministic equality support from other operations being impossible
Correctly explains what a secure enclave adds and how attestation works
Correctly articulates the trust/trade-off of enabling enclaves
