questions.title: Dynamic Data Masking: What It Actually Protects Against, and What It Doesn't
questions.prompt: A compliance officer wants Dynamic Data Masking applied to a CustomerSSN column and believes this 'encrypts' the data so it's protected at rest. Correct this misunderstanding: explain exactly what DDM does and does not do, at what layer it operates, and describe a specific, realistic way a user with ad-hoc query access could still exfiltrate the real unmasked values despite DDM being configured.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dynamic Data Masking is a presentation-layer control, not an encryption or at-rest protection mechanism. The actual bytes stored on disk for CustomerSSN are completely unchanged, in plaintext (or whatever encryption is separately applied, like TDE, which protects the physical files but not query results) — DDM only intercepts the result set returned to a query and substitutes a masking function's output for users who are not explicitly exempted from masking (members of db_owner, or any role/user granted the UNMASK permission, see the real value). This means DDM provides zero protection against anyone with sufficient permission to run arbitrary queries and who either already has UNMASK, is in db_owner, or who can get the underlying data to leave the masked column entirely.

A realistic exfiltration path despite DDM being configured: a user with ordinary SELECT permission (not UNMASK) runs a query that moves the SSN value through an expression before it's returned, for example SELECT CustomerSSN + '' or CAST(CustomerSSN AS varchar) concatenated with another column, or uses the value in a WHERE clause with a known candidate value — DDM is documented to be bypassable via inference attacks using range queries or brute-force guessing against a predictable value (a 9-digit SSN has, at most, a billion possibilities, and many fewer in practice given format rules), where the attacker repeatedly queries WHERE CustomerSSN = '<guess>' and observes whether a row is returned, narrowing down the real value without ever seeing it unmasked directly. Microsoft's own documentation explicitly warns DDM is not a substitute for proper access control or encryption and should always be combined with least-privilege permissions, auditing, and (for truly sensitive fields like SSN) Always Encrypted or column-level encryption if the goal is to actually prevent the value from being readable by unauthorized principals at all, including privileged ones.

So the correction for the compliance officer: DDM reduces accidental over-exposure for everyday users and reporting tools who have no business reason to see raw SSNs, but it is not encryption, doesn't protect data at rest, and does not stop a determined or sufficiently-privileged user from recovering the real value — either by being granted UNMASK, being in db_owner, or through inference/brute-force querying. For data this sensitive, DDM should be paired with, not substituted for, Always Encrypted and strict least-privilege access.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk the compliance officer back from 'encrypts' pretty directly: DDM doesn't touch the actual bytes on disk at all — the real SSN is sitting there completely unchanged, it's only the result set coming back from a query that gets substituted with a masked pattern, and only for users who aren't already exempt. Db_owners and anyone granted UNMASK see the real value every time, full stop.

To make it concrete, I'd show them this: take a user with plain SELECT access on the table, no UNMASK. They can't just select the column and see the SSN — fine. But they can run something like WHERE CustomerSSN = '123-45-6789' and watch whether a row comes back. Do that enough times with different guesses, and you can brute-force or narrow down the real SSN without ever seeing an unmasked value directly — that's a documented, known limitation of DDM, and Microsoft themselves say explicitly it's not meant to replace real encryption or access control.

What I'd recommend instead for something this sensitive: keep DDM if they want it for day-to-day protection against accidental over-exposure in reports and ad-hoc queries by people who have no reason to see raw SSNs, but for actual protection against a privileged or determined user recovering the value, they need Always Encrypted on that column and tightly scoped, audited access — DDM alone is not the control that gets them compliant for something like SSNs.
commonMistakes: Believing DDM encrypts the underlying data
Assuming DDM protects against any user with SELECT permission, not just non-exempt users
Not recognizing the WHERE-clause inference/brute-force bypass as a real, documented risk
Treating DDM as sufficient compliance control for highly sensitive fields like SSNs on its own
Forgetting that TDE (at rest) and DDM (presentation) solve completely different problems
keyPoints: DDM only changes what's returned in a query result set, not the underlying stored bytes
db_owner members and anyone with UNMASK permission always see real, unmasked values
DDM provides no protection for data at rest; that's a separate concern (TDE, encryption)
DDM is bypassable via inference/brute-force attacks using WHERE clause guessing
Microsoft explicitly documents DDM as a presentation control, not a substitute for encryption or access control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains DDM operates only on query result sets, not stored data
Correctly identifies who bypasses masking (db_owner, UNMASK) by default
Describes a concrete, realistic bypass/exfiltration method
Recommends appropriate complementary controls (Always Encrypted, least privilege)
Clarity in correcting the compliance officer's misunderstanding

questions.title: RPO and RTO: Translating Business Requirements Into an Actual HA/DR Design
questions.prompt: Define Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective precisely, in a way that distinguishes them from each other without ambiguity. Then explain why a business stakeholder saying 'we can't lose any data and we need to be back up instantly' is not actually an RPO/RTO requirement yet, and what you, as the DBA, need to get from them before you can pick between options like geo-replication, failover groups, and Always On Availability Groups.
questions.modelAnswer:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) answers: how much data, measured in time, are we willing to lose if a failure happens right now? If RPO is 5 minutes, it means the business accepts that in a disaster, up to 5 minutes of the most recent transactions might not exist in the recovered system — it's a measure of acceptable data loss, expressed as a time window, not a measure of speed. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) answers a completely different question: how long are we willing to be down — from the moment of failure to the moment the system is usable again? RTO is a measure of acceptable downtime duration, and it says nothing about how much data is in the system once it's back. These two numbers are independent: you can have a near-zero RPO (synchronous replication, no committed transaction is lost) paired with a long RTO (failover takes 30 minutes to execute and validate), or a long RPO (hourly snapshot backups) paired with a short RTO (restoring that snapshot is fast), or any other combination — one doesn't imply the other.

'We can't lose any data and need to be back up instantly' sounds like RPO=0 and RTO=0, but it's not a usable requirement yet because it hasn't been tested against reality or cost: true RPO=0 requires synchronous replication, which has real latency and throughput cost and specific failure-mode implications (if the secondary isn't reachable, do writes block, or does the primary continue async and risk data loss anyway?); true RTO≈0 requires automatic failover with health detection fast enough that applications barely notice, which costs more in infrastructure (multiple always-on replicas, likely cross-region) and still has some non-zero floor given DNS/connection-string propagation and application reconnection behavior. Until the stakeholder has actually weighed that cost and those trade-offs, 'zero and instant' is really just 'this is extremely important to us,' not a specified, costed number.

What I need from them before I can choose an architecture: a realistic, specific number for each — in minutes, not adjectives — ideally tied to what a real outage would cost per minute of downtime and per unit of data loss, so the number reflects actual business impact rather than an unexamined ideal. I also need to know the acceptable failure scope (single server, whole region, whole Azure outage) and whether they need this in a different geographic region (which pushes toward active geo-replication / auto-failover groups, inherently asynchronous across regions due to physics) versus same-region/zone (which allows synchronous Always On AG replicas with near-zero RPO). Only with real numbers and failure scope can I actually recommend, for example, Always On AG with a synchronous secondary in the same region for RTO measured in seconds and RPO near zero against a server/zone failure, versus auto-failover groups with geo-replication to a different region for surviving a full regional outage, where RPO will realistically be some small non-zero number because cross-region replication is asynchronous.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain RPO and RTO as answering two completely separate questions, and I always walk through both definitions explicitly because people genuinely conflate them. RPO is about data — if disaster strikes this second, how far back in time are we willing for our restored data to be? RTO is about time to recovery — from the moment things break, how long can the business tolerate being down before it's back up and usable? Neither one tells you anything about the other; you could be down for an hour but lose zero data, or be back up in thirty seconds but lose the last five minutes of transactions.

When a stakeholder says 'zero data loss, instant recovery,' I don't push back on the sentiment — that's clearly how important this system is to them — but I do push back on treating that as an actual spec, because it hasn't been priced or tested yet. True zero RPO means synchronous replication, which has real latency cost on every write and real decisions to make about what happens if the secondary goes unreachable. True zero RTO means automated failover fast enough that nobody notices, which means paying for standby capacity that's basically always running. Until they've seen what that costs and traded it off against the actual cost of an outage, 'instant and zero' is an aspiration, not a number I can design against.

So before I pick anything, I'm asking them for two real numbers in minutes — tied ideally to what an outage actually costs them per minute — and I'm asking what kind of failure they're protecting against: a single server dying, or an entire Azure region going dark. If it's same-region, I can get them close to zero RPO and a fast RTO with Always On AG synchronous replicas. If they genuinely need to survive a whole region disappearing, I'm talking about auto-failover groups with geo-replication, and I'll tell them upfront that cross-region replication is inherently asynchronous, so RPO in that scenario won't be a true zero no matter what we buy — it'll be small, but not zero, and I want them to agree to that number deliberately rather than discover it during a real outage.
commonMistakes: Treating RPO and RTO as the same concept or using them interchangeably
Accepting 'zero data loss, instant recovery' as a design spec without quantifying cost/trade-offs
Assuming synchronous replication is free or has no latency implications
Believing geo-replication across regions can achieve true zero RPO
Designing an HA/DR architecture before establishing the actual failure scope the business needs to survive
keyPoints: RPO measures acceptable data loss as a time window; RTO measures acceptable downtime duration
RPO and RTO are independent of each other and must be specified separately
'Zero and instant' is an aspiration, not a costed requirement, until trade-offs are examined
True near-zero RPO requires synchronous replication with real latency/throughput cost
Cross-region (geo) replication is inherently asynchronous, so cross-region RPO is never truly zero
Failure scope (server, zone, region) determines whether AG, failover groups, or geo-replication fits

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly and precisely defines RPO and RTO as distinct measures
Explains why the stated requirement isn't yet actionable/costed
Identifies the specific information needed (numbers, failure scope) before designing
Correctly maps failure scope to AG vs. failover groups/geo-replication
Clarity and business-communication framing

questions.title: What a PowerShell Pipeline Actually Passes Between Cmdlets
questions.prompt: A DBA coming from writing batch scripts assumes PowerShell's pipe operator works like it does in cmd.exe or bash — passing text output from one command into the next. Correct this: explain precisely what actually flows through the PowerShell pipeline, why that matters when you write Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'}, and what you lose if you instead parse the text output of a command the way you would in bash.
questions.modelAnswer:
In bash or cmd.exe, piping connects the standard output text stream of one program to the standard input text stream of the next — everything is just characters, and the receiving command has to parse that text to extract anything meaningful (field positions, delimiters, regex). PowerShell's pipeline is fundamentally different: it passes live .NET objects between cmdlets, not rendered text. Get-Service doesn't print a string table and hand text downstream — it emits a stream of ServiceController objects, each with real, strongly-typed properties (Name, Status, DisplayName, CanStop, etc.) still attached. When you write Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'}, Where-Object receives each actual ServiceController object one at a time, inspects its real .Status property (an enum value, not a string that merely looks like 'Running'), and only lets matching objects continue down the pipeline — there's no text parsing involved anywhere in that line.

This matters for a few concrete reasons: filtering/sorting/selecting by property is reliable because you're comparing actual typed values, not hoping a column lines up at the same character offset across different outputs (which breaks the moment a name field is longer than expected, locale changes a date format, or Microsoft tweaks the formatted output in an update); you can access properties and call methods on the object further down the pipeline that were never 'printed' as visible text at all — Get-Process | Sort-Object WorkingSet -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 sorts and filters using the real numeric WorkingSet property, something that would require careful column-aware text parsing in bash; and format cmdlets like Format-Table only come into play at the very end of a pipeline, for human display — they're not what's flowing between cmdlets, which is why inserting a Format-* cmdlet in the middle of a pipeline is a classic mistake that breaks everything downstream (it converts the objects into formatting instruction objects meant only for console rendering, not into usable data objects anymore).

If you instead treat PowerShell like bash and parse text output (for example piping through Out-String and then doing string splitting), you lose all of that type safety and the object's methods/properties beyond what happened to get printed, you become fragile to any change in display formatting, and you give up PowerShell's actual value proposition — which is that automation scripts can reliably act on structured data without writing brittle, locale- and version-sensitive text parsers.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell them straight away: forget everything you know about piping from bash, because PowerShell's pipe isn't moving text at all — it's moving real, live .NET objects with all their properties and methods still intact. When Get-Service runs, it's not printing a table that gets piped as characters — it's handing Where-Object actual ServiceController objects one by one, and Where-Object is checking a real property, $_.Status, which is an enum, not a string it had to extract from a column position.

That distinction is the whole reason PowerShell automation holds up over time in a way text-parsing scripts don't. If I write Get-Process | Sort-Object WorkingSet -Descending | Select-Object -First 5, I'm sorting on the actual numeric memory value as an object property — there's no column-width guessing, no locale-format breakage, none of the fragility you'd get trying to awk or cut your way through formatted text output. And I always warn people about one specific trap: Format-Table, Format-List, and friends only belong at the very end of a pipeline. The moment you stick one in the middle, you've converted your nice objects into display-only formatting objects, and everything after that in the pipeline breaks or behaves strangely, because there's no real data left to work with, just rendering instructions.

If someone insists on parsing text output the old bash way — piping through Out-String and splitting on spaces — I tell them they're throwing away the entire point of PowerShell. They lose type safety, they lose access to any property or method that wasn't part of what got printed, and they've built something that'll quietly break the next time a column gets a character wider or the display format changes in an update. The object pipeline is the actual feature; text parsing is a step backward into exactly the fragility PowerShell was built to eliminate.
commonMistakes: Assuming PowerShell pipes work like bash/cmd.exe text pipes
Inserting Format-Table or Format-List in the middle of a pipeline instead of at the end
Parsing PowerShell's formatted console output with string splitting instead of using the object properties directly
Believing $_.Status is a plain string rather than a typed property/enum
Assuming object-based filtering is slower or less reliable than text parsing
keyPoints: PowerShell pipes live .NET objects between cmdlets, not rendered text
Filtering/sorting operates on real, strongly-typed object properties, not parsed text columns
Format-* cmdlets convert objects to display-only output and should only appear at the end of a pipeline
Parsing text output (bash-style) loses type safety and is fragile to formatting/locale changes
Properties/methods not shown in console output are still fully usable further down the pipeline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that objects, not text, flow through the pipeline
Correctly explains the Get-Service | Where-Object example with real properties
Identifies the Format-* cmdlet mid-pipeline trap
Explains concretely what is lost by parsing text instead
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: SQL Authentication vs. Microsoft Entra Authentication: What Actually Changes
questions.prompt: Explain the real architectural difference between SQL Authentication and Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication against Azure SQL Database — not just 'one uses a password and one uses Azure AD,' but what each one means for credential storage, token lifetime, conditional access, and auditability. Then explain why a security-conscious DBA would push to eliminate SQL Authentication logins entirely wherever possible.
questions.modelAnswer:
SQL Authentication is self-contained within SQL Server/Azure SQL: a login's password hash is stored in the master database (or, for contained database users, in the user database itself), the server validates the password directly against that stored hash, and there is no external identity system involved at all — the credential's entire lifecycle (creation, rotation, expiration policy, lockout) is managed by SQL Server itself, with no integration into any organization-wide identity governance.

Microsoft Entra authentication is fundamentally different: the user or application authenticates against Entra ID first, and Azure SQL never sees a password at all — it receives and validates a signed, time-limited access token issued by Entra, which asserts the caller's identity and group memberships. This has several concrete consequences. Credential storage moves entirely out of the database: there's no password hash sitting in master to protect or leak. Token lifetime means access is inherently time-boxed — a stolen or cached token expires on its own schedule (commonly around an hour, with refresh tokens subject to the organization's own session policies), unlike a SQL login's password, which is valid indefinitely until someone manually changes it. Conditional Access becomes possible for database access specifically because Entra sits in the authentication path: an organization can require multi-factor authentication, block sign-in from untrusted locations or unmanaged devices, or require a compliant device, all enforced before Entra ever issues the token Azure SQL will accept — none of that is possible for a SQL login, which only ever checks a password. And auditability improves because every authentication event ties back to a real organizational identity in Entra (and can be correlated with Entra's own sign-in logs, MFA challenges, and Conditional Access evaluation results), rather than a shared or service-style SQL login whose actual human (or service) user may not be individually distinguishable in SQL Server's own audit trail.

A security-conscious DBA pushes to eliminate SQL Authentication logins wherever possible because every one of those benefits is simply unavailable to a password-based login: passwords can be shared, written down, reused across systems, phished, or brute-forced with no MFA in the way; a compromised SQL login's password keeps working until someone notices and manually rotates it, with no automatic expiration; and there's no way to apply Conditional Access policies to a bare SQL login no matter how mature the organization's Entra security posture is elsewhere. Realistically, SQL Authentication logins usually survive only for specific legacy application compatibility cases or non-Entra-aware tooling — everything else should move to Entra-based access, ideally through managed identities for applications and Entra groups for human access, so that joiner/mover/leaver identity lifecycle and access reviews happen through the organization's existing identity governance instead of being a separate, DBA-maintained password list.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always frame this as: SQL Authentication is the database being its own entire identity system, and Entra authentication is the database deliberately outsourcing that job to the organization's actual identity provider. With SQL auth, the password hash lives right there in master, SQL Server itself checks it, and that's the whole story — no outside system is involved, which also means no outside system's protections apply either.

With Entra auth, Azure SQL never even sees a password — it's handed a signed token that Entra already vouched for, and that token expires on its own, usually within about an hour. That short lifetime alone is a big deal operationally — a SQL login's password is valid forever until a human remembers to rotate it, but a leaked Entra token is only useful for a limited window. And because Entra sits in front of the whole thing, I can get Conditional Access in the picture — requiring MFA, blocking sign-in from outside the corporate network or from a device that isn't compliant — none of which is even a concept SQL Authentication understands, because it's just checking a password against a hash.

Auditability is the other piece I always bring up — with Entra, every connection ties back to a real identity I can trace through Entra's own sign-in logs, correlated with MFA and Conditional Access decisions. A shared SQL login, by contrast, is a black box — everyone using it looks identical in the logs.

So when I'm pushing to kill off SQL logins, it's not about SQL Authentication being 'weak' in isolation — a strong password with proper rotation is still a password — it's that it structurally can't plug into any of the organization's broader identity security investment. No MFA, no Conditional Access, no automatic expiration, no real per-person auditability. I'll keep a SQL login around only when something genuinely can't speak Entra, and even then I treat it as a tracked exception, not the default.
commonMistakes: Describing the difference as only 'passwords vs. Azure AD' without explaining the token/Conditional Access mechanics
Assuming MFA or Conditional Access can somehow be applied to a SQL login
Believing SQL Authentication passwords expire or rotate automatically the way Entra tokens do
Not recognizing that shared/service SQL logins degrade individual auditability
Assuming eliminating all SQL logins is always possible regardless of legacy application constraints
keyPoints: SQL Authentication stores and validates password hashes entirely within SQL Server, with no external identity involved
Entra authentication validates a signed, time-limited token issued by Entra; Azure SQL never sees a password
Conditional Access (MFA, device compliance, location) can only be enforced through Entra, never through SQL logins
Token-based access is inherently time-boxed, unlike indefinitely-valid SQL login passwords
Entra-based access ties to a real identity in centralized sign-in/audit logs; shared SQL logins obscure who actually connected

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the credential storage/validation difference
Correctly explains token lifetime implications
Correctly explains why Conditional Access only applies via Entra
Correctly explains the auditability improvement
Justifies eliminating SQL logins with realistic caveats

questions.title: PowerShell: Checking Backup Recency Across Every Database on an Instance
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell script (using dbatools) that connects to a SQL Server instance and reports every database whose most recent full backup is older than 24 hours, outputting the database name, last backup date, and hours since that backup, sorted with the stalest backups first. Explain why you chose the specific dbatools cmdlet you used over writing raw T-SQL and invoking it via Invoke-Sqlcmd.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core task is pulling backup history per database and computing an age, then filtering/sorting. dbatools' Get-DbaLastBackup is purpose-built for exactly this and already returns a strongly-typed object with LastFullBackup (and LastDiff/LastLog) as real DateTime objects per database, plus computed fields -- so the age computation and filtering logic in the script is simple PowerShell object manipulation rather than string-parsed T-SQL output. I pipe that output through Where-Object comparing against (Get-Date).AddHours(-24), then Sort-Object on the backup date ascending (oldest/stalest first), and format the three requested fields with Select-Object, computing HoursSinceBackup as a calculated property.

I chose Get-DbaLastBackup over raw T-SQL via Invoke-Sqlcmd for a few concrete reasons. First, Invoke-Sqlcmd returns a DataRow-based object whose column values and types depend entirely on how I wrote the T-SQL projection -- I'd have to hand-write and maintain the backup-history query myself (joining msdb..backupset and backupmediafamily correctly, handling the type codes for full/diff/log), where Get-DbaLastBackup already encodes that logic, tested across SQL Server versions, so I'm not re-deriving backup-type filtering logic that dbatools' maintainers have already solved. Second, Get-DbaLastBackup can take an array of instance names and iterate them in one call, which matters directly for Elastic-Jobs-style fleet checks across many servers -- I'm not writing my own foreach/connection-handling loop around Invoke-Sqlcmd for each box. Third, the returned objects are real PowerShell objects with typed DateTime properties, so 'hours since backup' is a plain TimeSpan subtraction, not date-string parsing that would be needed from a DataRow's raw column value.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move here is dbatools, not hand-rolled T-SQL, because this exact question -- when did each database last get backed up -- is something Get-DbaLastBackup already answers well, and I don't want to maintain my own query against msdb backup history tables when a well-tested cmdlet already does it correctly across SQL Server versions. I run it against the instance, and it hands me back one object per database with real DateTime properties for the last full, differential, and log backups.

From there it's just ordinary PowerShell object pipeline work -- I calculate hours since the last full backup as a property on each object, filter down to anything over 24 hours with Where-Object, and sort oldest-first so the worst offenders are at the top of the report. I'd explain the Invoke-Sqlcmd alternative like this: that cmdlet just runs T-SQL and hands back raw result rows -- I'd have to write and maintain the actual backup-history query myself, correctly joining the msdb system tables and handling backup type codes, and the result comes back as DataRow values I'd likely need to parse rather than already-typed DateTime objects I can subtract directly. And if I ever need to run this same check against twenty instances instead of one, Get-DbaLastBackup already accepts a list of SqlInstance values and loops them for me -- with Invoke-Sqlcmd I'd be writing that fan-out loop by hand.
commonMistakes: Writing a raw T-SQL query against msdb backup tables instead of using an existing, tested dbatools cmdlet
Comparing backup dates as strings instead of real DateTime objects
Forgetting to account for differential/log backups when the requirement is specifically about full backups
Not sorting so the stalest (most overdue) databases are easiest to spot first
Hardcoding a single instance name instead of allowing the script to scale to a list of instances
keyPoints: Get-DbaLastBackup returns typed DateTime properties per database for full/diff/log backups
Filtering/sorting is standard PowerShell object pipeline work (Where-Object, Sort-Object)
dbatools already encodes correct msdb backup-history query logic across SQL Server versions
Get-DbaLastBackup accepts multiple instances natively, useful for fleet-wide checks
Invoke-Sqlcmd requires hand-maintaining the T-SQL and parsing less-structured DataRow output

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working script using Get-DbaLastBackup (or justified equivalent)
Correctly computes hours since backup and filters >24 hours
Correctly sorts stalest backups first with the three requested fields
Clearly justifies dbatools cmdlet over raw Invoke-Sqlcmd T-SQL
Clean, idiomatic PowerShell

questions.title: Configuring Dynamic Data Masking with T-SQL on an Existing Table
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL to add Dynamic Data Masking to an existing Customers table: mask the Email column with the email masking function, mask the Phone column with a custom partial mask that shows only the last 4 digits, and mask SSN with the default masking function. Then write the T-SQL to grant a reporting role the ability to see unmasked SSN values without granting it broader permissions, and the T-SQL to verify a non-privileged login actually sees masked output.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each masking rule is applied with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = '...'), which attaches the masking metadata to the column without altering its data type or the underlying stored value. The email function (default()) specifically formats as the first letter plus XXX@XXX.com regardless of the real value's structure. For Phone, a partial mask gives control over exactly how many leading/trailing characters show and what fills the middle: partial(0,'XXX-XXX-',4) shows zero characters at the start, then the literal padding, then the last 4 real characters -- which satisfies 'only the last 4 digits' precisely. SSN uses the generic default() mask, which for a string type returns a fixed-length XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX regardless of the real value's actual length or content, which is the standard, un-customized obfuscation Microsoft documents for default().

Granting unmask access without broader permissions is done with GRANT UNMASK TO <role>, which is a narrow, standalone permission -- it does not imply or require db_owner, SELECT, or any other grant, and it can be revoked independently with REVOKE UNMASK. This is the deliberate design: UNMASK only affects whether masking is applied to values a principal is already otherwise permitted to see through other grants; it doesn't grant read access on its own.

To verify a non-privileged login actually sees masked output, I'd use EXECUTE AS USER = '<login_name>' (requiring IMPERSONATE permission, or just testing with an actual separate low-privilege connection) to run the SELECT as that identity, confirm the masked pattern appears instead of real values, then REVERT back to my own session -- running the SELECT as myself (likely db_owner or sysadmin) would be meaningless since those roles always bypass masking regardless of any DDM configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd handle each column with its own ALTER TABLE ... ADD MASKED WITH statement -- that's the whole mechanism, and it's non-destructive, it just tags the column with masking metadata, the real value underneath never changes. For email I'd use the built-in email() function since that's exactly what it's designed for. For phone, since the requirement is specifically 'only show the last 4 digits,' I reach for partial() and set it up so zero characters show at the start, I control what the padding looks like in the middle, and exactly 4 real characters show at the end. For SSN, default() is the right call since there's no customization requested -- it just gives the standard fixed masked pattern for that data type.

For the reporting role needing to see real SSNs, I'd specifically avoid reaching for anything broader than GRANT UNMASK TO that role -- that permission exists precisely so I'm not forced to hand out db_owner or extra SELECT grants just to unmask a column, and I can pull it back cleanly later with REVOKE UNMASK if their need changes.

And to actually prove this works rather than just assume it, I always test as the actual low-privilege identity -- either a real separate connection logged in as that user, or EXECUTE AS USER if I have IMPERSONATE rights, run the exact SELECT, and confirm I'm seeing the masked pattern, not the real data. I wouldn't trust testing this under my own session, because as db_owner or sysadmin I'd see real values regardless of what masking is configured -- that's not a meaningful test of what DDM is actually doing for everyone else.
commonMistakes: Assuming ADD MASKED WITH changes the actual stored value
Using default() for phone when the requirement calls for a specific partial mask
Granting db_owner or broad SELECT instead of the narrow UNMASK permission
Testing masked behavior under a sysadmin/db_owner session, which always bypasses masking
Forgetting GRANT UNMASK can be scoped and later revoked independently
keyPoints: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH attaches masking without changing stored data
partial() mask gives explicit control over prefix/suffix character counts and padding
GRANT UNMASK is a standalone permission, independent of SELECT/db_owner
UNMASK only affects masking, not underlying read access, which must already be granted separately
Testing masked output must be done as the actual non-privileged principal, not as db_owner/sysadmin

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct DDM syntax for all three columns (email, custom partial phone, default SSN)
Correct GRANT UNMASK statement scoped narrowly to the reporting role
Correct verification method using a non-privileged identity
Explains why db_owner/sysadmin testing is invalid

questions.title: Query Store: Finding and Force-Fixing a Regressed Query Plan
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL against Query Store's catalog views to find queries whose average duration has gotten at least 3x worse in the last day compared to the prior week, and then write the T-SQL to force the better of two known plans for the worst offender. Explain what forcing a plan actually does and does not guarantee going forward.
questions.modelAnswer:
Query Store exposes per-plan, per-time-interval runtime statistics in sys.query_store_runtime_stats, linked to sys.query_store_plan (which plan), sys.query_store_query (which logical query), and sys.query_store_query_text (the actual text), bucketed by sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval. To find regressions, I aggregate average duration for a recent interval (last 24 hours) and compare it against the average for an earlier baseline interval (the prior week), joining on query_id, and filter to where recent_avg >= 3 * baseline_avg. This requires being careful to aggregate avg_duration weighted by execution count (or just compare straight averages if execution counts are roughly comparable) across potentially multiple plans and multiple runtime_stats_interval rows per plan within each time window.

Once I've identified the worst offender's query_id, I'd look at sys.query_store_plan for that query_id to find a known-good historical plan_id (one whose historical average duration was much better), and then call sys.sp_query_store_force_plan (@query_id, @plan_id) to force it.

Forcing a plan guarantees the optimizer will use that specific plan shape for that query going forward -- it pins the plan rather than letting the optimizer re-choose, as long as the plan remains valid (the schema hasn't changed in a way that invalidates it, e.g., a referenced index being dropped). It does NOT guarantee that plan will stay optimal forever: if the underlying data distribution shifts significantly (a table grows 50x, or a previously rare value becomes extremely common), the forced plan can become the wrong choice again, and forcing doesn't adapt to that -- it has to be manually revisited. It also does not retroactively fix already-cached bad plans elsewhere unless they share the same query_id/plan_id mechanism, and it's a per-query action, not a global, set-it-and-forget-it fix, so I'd still want monitoring in place (re-running this same regression query periodically) to catch when a forced plan itself eventually becomes the regression.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My approach is to go straight at Query Store's runtime stats views -- that's literally what they're there for. I pull average duration for the most recent day and the prior week, grouped by query_id, and look for anywhere the recent number is at least three times worse than the baseline. I have to be a little careful joining across sys.query_store_runtime_stats and its interval table since a query can have multiple plans and multiple time buckets, but the core idea is just comparing two averages.

Once I've got the worst offender's query_id, I go look at its plan history in sys.query_store_plan to find a plan_id that used to perform well, and then I force it with sp_query_store_force_plan -- one call, two parameters, query_id and plan_id.

The thing I always make sure people understand about forcing a plan: it's not magic, and it's not permanent protection. What it actually does is pin the optimizer to use that specific plan shape going forward, as long as that plan is still valid -- if someone drops an index the plan depends on, forcing breaks and SQL Server falls back to choosing a new plan. What it doesn't do is adapt if the data itself changes dramatically later -- if that table grows fifty times bigger, the plan I forced today because it was fast might become the wrong choice six months from now, and forcing won't notice that on its own. It's a targeted fix for right now, not a forever guarantee, so I'd keep re-running this regression check periodically rather than treating one force_plan call as the end of the story.
questions.example:
SELECT q.query_id, AVG(rs.avg_duration) AS avg_dur
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval rsi ON rs.runtime_stats_interval_id = rsi.runtime_stats_interval_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query q ON p.query_id = q.query_id
WHERE rsi.start_time >= DATEADD(DAY, -1, SYSUTCDATETIME())
GROUP BY q.query_id;

-- Force the better known plan:
EXEC sys.sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 482, @plan_id = 519;
commonMistakes: Comparing total duration instead of average duration, skewing results by execution count
Not joining through the interval table, mixing up time windows incorrectly
Assuming sp_query_store_force_plan permanently guarantees good performance regardless of future data changes
Forcing a plan without first confirming it actually performed better historically
Treating a single force_plan action as a substitute for ongoing monitoring
keyPoints: Regression detection compares recent average duration against a prior baseline per query_id
sys.query_store_runtime_stats joined with plan/query/text catalog views provides the needed data
sp_query_store_force_plan pins a specific plan_id for a query_id going forward
Forcing a plan does not adapt to future data distribution changes
Forcing only remains effective while the plan stays valid (e.g., referenced indexes still exist)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct regression-detection query using Query Store catalog views
Correct use of sp_query_store_force_plan with appropriate query_id/plan_id
Correctly explains what forcing a plan guarantees
Correctly explains what forcing a plan does NOT guarantee (data drift, validity)
