questions.title: A PowerShell Maintenance Script Reports Success But Didn't Actually Do Anything
questions.prompt: A scheduled PowerShell script that's supposed to shrink log files on a list of databases has been running every night, exiting with code 0, and logging 'Completed successfully' — but the log files it's supposed to shrink are not actually getting smaller. Walk through why a script can report success while doing nothing meaningful, the specific PowerShell habits that cause this, and how you'd rewrite it to fail loudly instead.
questions.modelAnswer:
The most common root cause of 'reports success but does nothing' in PowerShell is that a cmdlet inside the script is throwing a non-terminating error, which by default does NOT stop script execution and does NOT cause the script's own exit code to reflect failure -- PowerShell happily continues to the next line, eventually reaches the end of the script, and exits with code 0 because, as far as the PowerShell host is concerned, nothing told it to do otherwise. If the script is written with try/catch around individual operations but the actual failing cmdlet is one whose errors are non-terminating by default (many cmdlets only throw terminating errors for certain categories of failure, not all), the catch block never fires, because there's nothing being thrown into it to catch -- the error is written to the error stream and execution just moves on.

A second, closely related cause: if the script invokes T-SQL via Invoke-Sqlcmd or a similar mechanism and that call fails (permission denied, object doesn't exist, wrong database context), depending on the specific cmdlet and its parameters, the failure might only be visible in the error stream or a return value the script never actually checks -- a script that doesn't inspect $? after an operation, doesn't check an explicit return/exit code, and doesn't have $ErrorActionPreference set to 'Stop' can sail through a failed operation as if it succeeded, because nothing in the script's own logic is actually verifying that the operation did what it claimed.

Third, and specific to this scenario: a script that logs 'Completed successfully' unconditionally at the very end, regardless of what happened in between, is structurally guaranteed to report success every time, because that log line was never actually gated on verifying any real outcome -- it's just the last line of the script, reached as long as nothing fatal stopped execution entirely.

To rewrite this to fail loudly, I'd: set $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' at the top of the script (or pass -ErrorAction Stop to individual risky cmdlets) so that normally-non-terminating errors become terminating ones the script's own try/catch can actually see and react to; wrap the actual shrink operations in try/catch and, in the catch block, write a clear error, set a non-zero exit code, and stop further processing of that database (or the whole script, depending on severity) rather than silently moving to log success; and critically, VERIFY the actual outcome rather than trusting that 'the command ran without visibly erroring' means 'it worked' -- for a log shrink specifically, that means querying sys.database_files or DBCC SQLPERF(LOGSPACE) before and after the shrink operation and asserting the size actually decreased (or logging a specific, honest 'ran but had no effect' result if it didn't, which is meaningfully different from both success and a hard failure, and should be visible as its own outcome, not folded into a generic 'completed successfully').
questions.professionalAnswer:
Nine times out of ten when I see a script that claims success but visibly didn't do anything, the root cause is non-terminating errors. A lot of PowerShell cmdlets, by default, don't actually stop the script when something goes wrong -- they write to the error stream and just keep going, and the script reaches its last line and exits 0 because nothing ever told PowerShell this was a failure. If there's a try/catch in there, it doesn't even help, because catch only fires on terminating errors, and a lot of real failures in PowerShell just... aren't terminating by default.

The other thing I always suspect in a script like this is the actual T-SQL execution step — if it's calling Invoke-Sqlcmd or something similar and that call fails for a permissions or object-not-found reason, whether that failure actually stops anything depends entirely on whether the script set ErrorAction to Stop and whether it checks the result afterward. A script that just assumes 'if it got this far, it worked' is exactly the pattern that produces a false success log.

And the smoking gun in this specific case is that 'Completed successfully' line — if that's unconditionally the last line of the script with nothing actually gating it on a real check of outcome, of course it always prints. It's not reporting success, it's reporting 'reached the end of the file.'

To fix it, I'd set $ErrorActionPreference to Stop right at the top so errors actually become catchable, wrap the real work in proper try/catch that sets a real non-zero exit code and stops on failure instead of quietly moving on, and — this is the part people skip — actually verify the result. For a log shrink specifically, that means checking the log file size before and after and asserting it actually got smaller, not just trusting that the shrink command didn't visibly error. If it ran clean but genuinely had no effect, that's its own distinct, honestly-logged outcome, not something I'd fold into 'completed successfully.'
commonMistakes: Assuming try/catch alone guarantees errors will be caught, regardless of error type
Not setting $ErrorActionPreference or -ErrorAction Stop on risky operations
Logging success unconditionally at the end of a script rather than gating it on verified outcome
Trusting that a cmdlet 'not visibly erroring' means the intended operation actually happened
Not distinguishing 'ran with no effect' from both 'succeeded' and 'failed' as a reportable outcome
keyPoints: Non-terminating errors by default don't stop script execution or affect the exit code
try/catch only catches terminating errors; many cmdlet failures are non-terminating by default
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' converts non-terminating errors into catchable terminating ones
An unconditional 'completed successfully' log line at the end of a script guarantees a false-positive success report
Real verification requires checking actual outcome (log file size before/after), not just absence of visible errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains non-terminating vs. terminating error behavior in PowerShell
Correctly identifies $ErrorActionPreference/-ErrorAction Stop as part of the fix
Correctly identifies the unconditional success log line as a structural bug
Proposes real outcome verification (before/after size check), not just error absence
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Troubleshooting a Login That Works in SSMS But Fails From the Application
questions.prompt: A service account can connect to Azure SQL Database fine from SSMS on your machine, but the production application using the exact same login fails with a permission error on one specific stored procedure call. Walk through the specific, non-obvious reasons this happens even though 'it's the same login,' and how you'd isolate which one applies here.
questions.modelAnswer:
The phrase 'exact same login' hides several differences that commonly explain this exact symptom. First, and most common: the application and SSMS may be connecting to different databases entirely, or the same database but the login's associated database user has different permissions than expected in that specific database context -- a login can exist at the server level but have a contained database user mapped in one database with certain role memberships, and no mapping (or different role memberships) in another database the application actually targets. I'd check this first by confirming, from the application's own connection string, the exact database (and server, if there's any chance of a failover group or multiple environments) it's connecting to, not assuming it matches what I tested in SSMS.

Second, execution context inside the stored procedure itself: if the procedure references objects in another database or schema, or calls EXECUTE AS within its own definition, or the procedure was created with a specific owner whose permissions are what actually matter (ownership chaining) rather than the calling login's direct permissions, the calling login's own grants might be irrelevant to whether the proc succeeds -- what matters is whether the chain of ownership/execution context resolves permissions the way everyone assumes. I'd check the procedure's actual definition for EXECUTE AS, cross-database/cross-schema references, and ownership, since 'permission error on one specific procedure' (not a broad permission failure) often points to something specific to that one object's definition rather than a login-wide problem.

Third, and specifically relevant for Azure SQL with Entra authentication: if the application authenticates via a managed identity or an Entra service principal rather than literally the same SQL login credential I used in SSMS, 'same login' might not be as literal as it sounds -- a managed identity resolves to its own distinct database principal with its own grants, separate from a human Entra account or SQL login that happens to share a similar-sounding name, and I'd explicitly verify, via sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members, which actual principal the application's connection maps to versus which principal my SSMS session maps to -- they may not be the identical principal at all despite both being described informally as 'the service account.'

Fourth, parameter/context differences: if the stored procedure's logic branches based on something like SUSER_NAME(), ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), or application-supplied parameters that differ between my manual SSMS test and what the real application actually passes, the procedure could be failing a permission check inside its own logic (not a SQL-engine-level GRANT/DENY) that only triggers for certain input -- so I'd also compare whether I'm calling the procedure with genuinely identical parameters, not just 'as the same login.'

To isolate which applies, I'd: confirm the exact database/server the application targets and reconnect SSMS to that exact same target; query sys.database_principals / sys.database_role_members for both my SSMS session's actual resolved principal and (via application logging or a DBA trace) the application's actual resolved principal, to confirm they're truly identical; and inspect the procedure's definition for EXECUTE AS/ownership chaining/cross-database references before assuming the problem is login-level permissions at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The phrase that always makes me suspicious here is 'exact same login' — in practice that phrase hides a lot of ways things can actually be different. My first check is whether the application is even connecting to the same database I tested in SSMS — a login can have completely different permissions depending on which database's user mapping actually applies, and it's easy to test in SSMS against one environment while the app is quietly pointed at another.

If the database genuinely matches, I go look at the stored procedure's own definition next, because a failure on one specific procedure rather than a broad permission error usually means something about that procedure itself, not the login overall. Does it use EXECUTE AS inside its body? Does it reference objects in another schema or database? Ownership chaining means the permissions that actually matter for that cross-reference might belong to the procedure's owner, not to whoever's calling it — so the calling login's own grants can be completely beside the point.

In Azure SQL specifically, I also ask whether the application is actually authenticating the same way I am. If it's using a managed identity or a service principal and I tested with a SQL login or my own Entra account, those are genuinely different principals under the hood even if everyone's been casually calling both of them 'the service account' — I'd go check sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members for both and confirm they're actually the same object, not just similarly named.

And finally, I check whether the procedure's logic itself branches on something like the caller's identity or specific parameter values — because if it does, this might not be a GRANT/DENY problem at the engine level at all, it might be the procedure's own internal logic rejecting a specific input the app happens to send that I never tested manually. I'd walk through all four of these in order rather than assuming the first plausible one is the real answer.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'same login name' guarantees identical effective permissions across databases
Not checking the stored procedure's definition for EXECUTE AS or ownership chaining
Assuming a managed identity and a similarly-named SQL login are the same underlying principal
Testing with different parameters than the application actually sends and assuming that's equivalent
Jumping to re-granting broad permissions without isolating the actual cause first
keyPoints: Login/user mapping can differ by database — confirm the application targets the exact same database
Ownership chaining/EXECUTE AS inside the procedure can make the owner's permissions, not the caller's, the deciding factor
Managed identity/service principal authentication resolves to a distinct principal from a human/Entra account with a similar name
sys.database_principals and sys.database_role_members should be used to confirm both sessions resolve to the truly identical principal
The procedure's own internal logic (not just GRANT/DENY) can reject specific parameter values or identities

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies database-specific user mapping as a candidate cause
Correctly explains ownership chaining/EXECUTE AS as a procedure-specific cause
Correctly distinguishes managed identity/service principal from a similarly-named login
Identifies procedure-internal logic/parameter differences as a possible cause
Describes a sound isolation method (sys.database_principals, role_members, proc definition)

questions.title: Designing an Always On Availability Group Topology for a Multi-Region DR Requirement
questions.prompt: A client runs SQL Server on Azure VMs (not Azure SQL Database) for a legacy application that can't move to PaaS yet. They need: zero data loss for a same-datacenter server failure, and survival of an entire region outage with an acceptable, pre-agreed small amount of data loss. Design the Always On Availability Group topology — replica count, synchronous vs. asynchronous commit per replica, and automatic vs. manual failover per replica — that satisfies both requirements, and explain why a single topology can satisfy both.
questions.modelAnswer:
This requires at least three replicas across two distinct failure domains: two replicas in the primary region (the current primary plus at least one secondary, both configured for synchronous commit with automatic failover between them), and a third replica in a secondary Azure region configured for asynchronous commit with manual failover only.

The two same-region replicas satisfy the first requirement directly: synchronous commit means a transaction isn't acknowledged as committed to the client until it's hardened on both the primary and the synchronous secondary, so a failure of the primary server alone (not the whole datacenter/region) loses zero committed transactions — the secondary already has everything, and automatic failover (requiring a third quorum-contributing element, typically a file share witness or the cluster's own quorum mechanism, since Windows Server Failover Clustering needs quorum to safely automate failover decisions) can promote it without a human needing to intervene, usually within seconds.

The cross-region replica satisfies the second requirement specifically because it is NOT synchronous — synchronous commit across regions would mean every transaction waits on a round-trip to a different Azure region before being acknowledged, which adds real, likely unacceptable latency to every single write for a workload that otherwise doesn't need it; asynchronous commit lets the primary acknowledge transactions locally and ship them to the cross-region replica without blocking on it, which is exactly why cross-region HA/DR setups accept a small RPO rather than zero — there's always some number of transactions in flight that haven't yet reached the async replica when a true regional disaster strikes. Manual failover (rather than automatic) is deliberately chosen for the cross-region replica because a region-wide outage is a major, consequential event that should involve a human decision (confirming the primary region is actually down, not just experiencing a transient network partition that would make failing over unnecessary and disruptive) and because the automatic-failover quorum mechanics that work cleanly within one region's low-latency network don't translate safely to blindly automating a decision across regions with higher, variable latency.

One topology satisfies both requirements because the two concerns are decomposed onto different replicas with different settings rather than forcing one blended compromise: the in-region pair is tuned entirely for the zero-data-loss, fast-automatic-failover requirement, and the cross-region replica is tuned entirely for the 'survive losing an entire region, with an accepted small RPO' requirement, and Always On Availability Groups explicitly support mixing synchronous and asynchronous replicas with different failover modes within the same group, rather than requiring every replica to share one policy.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this as three replicas, not two, because the two requirements genuinely need different replication behavior and trying to satisfy both with one setting would mean compromising on one of them. In the primary region, I'd put the current primary and one synchronous secondary, with automatic failover between the two — synchronous commit means a transaction isn't considered done until both copies have it, so losing just the primary server doesn't lose any committed data, and automatic failover through the cluster's quorum mechanism means that happens without anyone picking up a phone.

Then a third replica goes in a different Azure region entirely, and that one is asynchronous with manual failover, very deliberately. Asynchronous because making every write wait on a round-trip to another region would tank write performance for a workload that doesn't otherwise need that latency — so I'm trading a small, agreed amount of possible data loss for keeping normal operations fast. Manual failover because a whole-region outage is the kind of event I actually want a human eyeballing before triggering — confirming this is real and not some transient blip — and automated quorum-based failover decisions that work great within one low-latency region don't translate cleanly across a higher-latency, cross-region link.

The reason one topology handles both requirements is that I'm not trying to force one replication setting to do two jobs — I'm assigning each requirement to the replica pair that's actually suited for it. Always On is explicitly built to let you mix sync and async replicas with different failover modes in the same availability group, so this isn't a workaround, it's exactly the intended use of the feature for this kind of layered HA/DR requirement.
commonMistakes: Using synchronous commit across regions, adding unacceptable write latency
Using automatic failover for the cross-region replica without accounting for quorum/latency risk
Assuming two replicas (one sync, one async) is sufficient without a true in-region automatic-failover pair
Believing a single availability group can't mix synchronous and asynchronous replica settings
Not recognizing that zero-RPO and regional survival are two separate requirements needing separate replica settings
keyPoints: Three replicas: two same-region (synchronous, automatic failover), one cross-region (asynchronous, manual failover)
Synchronous commit guarantees zero data loss for a same-region server-level failure
Automatic failover requires quorum, which is reliable within a single low-latency region
Asynchronous commit across regions avoids adding cross-region latency to every write
Manual failover for the cross-region replica reflects the judgment call a regional disaster requires
Always On supports mixing sync/async and automatic/manual settings within a single availability group

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the three-replica topology with appropriate commit modes
Correctly explains why synchronous commit satisfies the zero-data-loss same-region requirement
Correctly explains why asynchronous commit is required cross-region and its RPO implication
Correctly justifies manual failover for the cross-region replica
Explains why one topology can satisfy both requirements via decomposition

questions.title: Auto-Failover Groups vs. Active Geo-Replication: Choosing the Right Tool
questions.prompt: A client has 40 databases on a single Azure SQL logical server and wants disaster recovery to a secondary region. Another team in the same company runs 3 critical databases that each need independent, fine-grained control over which specific secondary region they replicate to, with different failover timing for each database. Design the DR approach for each team and justify why auto-failover groups suit one and active geo-replication suits the other, including what you'd lose by using the wrong one for each case.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the first team's 40 databases on one logical server, an auto-failover group is the correct fit specifically because it operates at the server level: you configure the group once, between the primary server and a single secondary server, and every database on that server (current and future, since failover groups can be configured to include all databases on the server automatically) replicates and fails over together, as a single unit, through one stable listener endpoint. This is exactly the right shape for '40 databases that should all move to the same secondary region together, consistently, without needing per-database configuration' — it dramatically reduces operational overhead versus configuring and monitoring 40 separate replication relationships, and automatic failover with a single grace period policy applies uniformly.

For the second team's 3 databases, active geo-replication (configured per-database, outside the failover-group construct) is the correct fit specifically because it allows each database to have its own independent secondary — potentially in different regions from each other — and its own readable secondary count/configuration, without being tied to what any other database (on the same or a different server) is doing. Active geo-replication also, notably, supports up to four secondaries per database (useful for read-scale fanout in addition to DR) versus a failover group's simpler primary/secondary-pair shape, and because it's configured per database, failover timing and the decision to fail over can genuinely be made independently per database rather than as an all-or-nothing group action.

What you'd lose using the wrong one for each case: if the 40-database team used active geo-replication instead of a failover group, they'd have to configure and separately monitor 40 individual replication relationships, there'd be no single listener endpoint abstracting 'where the primary currently is' for application connection strings (each database's own endpoint would need separate handling), and failing over 40 databases consistently together during a real incident would require either careful manual orchestration or custom automation that a failover group gives you for free. If the 3-critical-database team used a single auto-failover group instead, they'd be forced into one shared secondary server/region for all three and one shared failover policy/grace period, losing the ability to send one database to a different region than another or to fail over one independently without affecting the other two — exactly the fine-grained, independent control their requirement explicitly calls for.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the 40-database team, I'm reaching straight for an auto-failover group, because it's built exactly for this shape of problem — it operates at the server level, so I configure the relationship once between the primary and secondary server, and every database on that server rides along as a unit through one listener endpoint. Trying to manage 40 individual geo-replication relationships instead would mean 40 things to configure, 40 things to monitor, and no single abstraction for 'where is the primary right now' that the application layer can just point at.

For the 3 critical databases that each need to go to potentially different regions with independently-controlled failover timing, that's precisely where a failover group stops being the right tool, because a group ties everything on that server to one shared secondary and one shared failover policy. Active geo-replication configured per database is what gives this team the actual independence they're asking for — each database can have its own secondary region, its own readable-secondary setup, even up to four secondaries if they wanted read-scale on top of DR, and failing one over doesn't force the other two to move with it.

If I swapped these — forced the 40-database team onto individual geo-replication, or crammed the 3 independent-requirement databases into one shared failover group — I'd be creating exactly the problem each team is trying to avoid. The 40-database team would lose the operational simplicity that's the whole point of using a group at that scale, and the 3-database team would lose the per-database regional and timing independence that's explicitly their actual requirement, forcing all three onto one secondary region and one failover decision whether they like it or not.
commonMistakes: Assuming active geo-replication and failover groups are interchangeable regardless of scale or independence needs
Forcing many databases into separate geo-replication relationships instead of one failover group
Forcing databases that need independent regions/timing into one shared failover group
Forgetting that failover groups provide a listener endpoint that per-database geo-replication does not
Not recognizing active geo-replication's multi-secondary (up to 4) read-scale capability
keyPoints: Auto-failover groups operate at the server level, covering all (or all-configured) databases as a single unit
Active geo-replication is configured per database, allowing independent secondary regions and timing
Failover groups provide one stable listener endpoint, simplifying application connection strings at scale
Active geo-replication supports up to four secondaries per database, useful for read-scale beyond just DR
Using a failover group for databases needing independent regions/timing forces them into one shared policy
Using per-database geo-replication for a large uniform fleet multiplies operational/monitoring overhead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends failover group for the 40-database uniform fleet with justification
Correctly recommends active geo-replication for the 3 independent databases with justification
Correctly explains server-level vs. per-database scope distinction
Correctly explains the operational cost of choosing the wrong tool in each case
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Choosing Between Provisioned vCore, Serverless, and Hyperscale for Three Different Workloads
questions.prompt: You're advising on compute tier selection for three Azure SQL Database workloads: (1) a steady, 24/7 high-throughput OLTP system with predictable load, (2) an internal reporting database used in bursts during business hours on weekdays only, largely idle overnight and weekends, and (3) a rapidly-growing database currently at 800GB that's expected to reach several terabytes within a year and occasionally needs near-instant restores for testing. Recommend a tier for each and justify why the other two tiers would be a worse fit for that specific workload.
questions.modelAnswer:
For workload (1), the steady 24/7 high-throughput OLTP system, provisioned vCore (General Purpose, or Business Critical if latency/IO characteristics demand it) is the right fit: provisioned compute means a fixed, dedicated amount of vCores and memory are allocated continuously, which is exactly aligned with a workload that's actually using capacity nearly all the time — you're paying a predictable rate for capacity you're genuinely consuming around the clock. Serverless would be a poor fit here because its value proposition is auto-pausing and auto-scaling during idle/variable periods — for a workload with no idle periods to speak of, serverless's auto-scale overhead (and its per-second compute billing model, which is specifically designed to save money by scaling DOWN during idle time) provides no benefit and can actually cost more than provisioned pricing for sustained, predictable high usage, since serverless's pricing model is built around variability, not steady saturation. Hyperscale would also be a worse fit unless this workload also has unusual storage-scale or backup/restore-speed needs — Hyperscale's real differentiator is its distributed storage architecture, which matters most when storage size or backup/restore speed is the actual bottleneck, not raw sustained compute throughput, so choosing it here would add complexity without addressing this workload's actual characteristic.

For workload (2), the business-hours-only reporting database, serverless is the right fit precisely because its core mechanism — auto-pausing compute during sustained inactivity and auto-scaling vCores within a configured min/max range based on actual load — directly matches a workload that's predictably idle for large stretches (nights, weekends) and only needs real compute during business hours. Billing based on vCores actually used per second, plus near-zero cost during the paused state, means you're not paying full provisioned rate for capacity sitting unused the majority of the week. Provisioned vCore would be a worse fit because you'd be paying for the same fixed capacity 24/7 regardless of the fact that most of that time, little or nothing is happening — you'd be funding idle compute most of the week. Hyperscale isn't the right lens for this decision at all, since the deciding factor here is compute utilization pattern, not storage scale.

For workload (3), the rapidly-growing multi-terabyte database needing fast restores for testing, Hyperscale is the right fit precisely because of its distributed, page-server storage architecture: it scales storage independently of compute, into many terabytes, without the downtime a storage resize forces on General Purpose/Business Critical, and its backup/restore mechanism is near-instant snapshot-based rather than a traditional backup job whose duration scales with database size — which directly addresses 'occasionally needs near-instant restores for testing' in a way neither other tier can match (a multi-terabyte database's restore time on General Purpose/Business Critical scales up substantially with size, which is precisely the problem Hyperscale's architecture was built to solve). Provisioned vCore (General Purpose/Business Critical) would be a worse fit as the database grows, both because of the eventual storage ceiling and because restore times would keep getting worse as the database grows toward multiple terabytes. Serverless would be a particularly poor fit here, since serverless is about compute elasticity for variable load, and says nothing about solving the storage-scale or restore-speed problem this workload actually has — picking it would mean solving the wrong axis of the problem entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the steady 24/7 OLTP system, I'd go provisioned vCore without much hesitation — that workload is using real capacity basically all the time, so a fixed, dedicated allocation at a predictable rate is exactly what matches it. Serverless would be solving a problem this workload doesn't have — there's no meaningful idle time for auto-pause or auto-scale to actually save money on, and Hyperscale's whole value is around storage architecture, which isn't really this workload's bottleneck unless there's something else going on with its data size.

For the business-hours-only reporting database, that's almost a textbook serverless case — it's predictably idle most of the week, and serverless auto-pauses during that idle time and auto-scales up for the bursts during business hours, so I'm not paying a full provisioned rate around the clock for capacity that's mostly sitting there doing nothing nights and weekends. Provisioned vCore would mean paying full price for all that unused time, which is exactly the cost serverless exists to avoid.

And for the rapidly-growing, multi-terabyte database that needs fast test restores, Hyperscale is the one actual fit here, because the real problem isn't compute at all — it's storage scale and restore speed, and that's specifically what Hyperscale's distributed storage architecture was built to solve, with near-instant snapshot-based restores regardless of size and storage scaling that doesn't force downtime the way a resize would on the other tiers. Provisioned vCore would just get slower to restore and more constrained as this thing grows toward multiple terabytes, and serverless doesn't even address the actual bottleneck — it's solving a compute-elasticity problem for a workload whose real issue is storage and restore speed.
commonMistakes: Recommending serverless for a steady, always-busy workload
Recommending provisioned vCore for a predictably idle, bursty workload without considering serverless cost savings
Recommending Hyperscale based on raw throughput needs rather than storage scale/restore-speed needs
Assuming Hyperscale is simply 'a bigger vCore tier' rather than a different storage architecture
Not addressing why the other two tiers are specifically worse for each workload, only naming one tier per case
keyPoints: Provisioned vCore fits steady, continuously-high-utilization workloads at a predictable rate
Serverless auto-pauses/auto-scales compute, fitting workloads with predictable idle periods
Hyperscale's differentiator is distributed storage, delivering fast restores independent of database size
Serverless provides no benefit (and can cost more) for workloads with no real idle time
Provisioned tiers' restore time scales with database size, unlike Hyperscale's snapshot-based restores
Matching the tier to the workload's actual bottleneck (compute utilization pattern vs. storage scale) is the deciding factor

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends provisioned vCore for workload 1 with sound justification
Correctly recommends serverless for workload 2 with sound justification
Correctly recommends Hyperscale for workload 3 with sound justification
Explains why the other two tiers are worse fits for each specific workload
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Designing a Defense-in-Depth Security Architecture for a Database Holding Regulated PII
questions.prompt: Design the full security architecture for an Azure SQL Database holding healthcare records subject to strict compliance requirements: patient SSNs, diagnosis codes, and billing data. Specify which control handles which threat (network-level unauthorized access, a compromised application credential, a privileged insider, data at rest theft, and after-the-fact audit/forensics), explaining why no single control covers all five threats and must be layered with the others.
questions.modelAnswer:
Five distinct threats require five distinct, complementary controls, because each control operates at a different layer and is blind to threats outside its own layer:

1. Network-level unauthorized access (someone trying to reach the database who shouldn't be able to at all): handled by private endpoints/VNet integration plus server firewall rules, which determine who can even establish a network connection to the server in the first place, before any authentication happens. This control is irrelevant to someone who already has valid, legitimate network access — it only stops reaching the database at all.

2. A compromised application credential (an attacker who has stolen the application's connection credential/managed identity token but isn't a human insider): handled primarily by least-privilege permissions scoped tightly to exactly what the application needs (no more), combined with Entra-based authentication's shorter token lifetimes limiting how long a stolen credential remains useful, and Row-Level Security if the application's own logic is what's supposed to restrict which patients' records a given context can see — RLS enforces that restriction at the database engine level even if the compromised credential is used to craft a query that tries to read beyond what the legitimate application would normally request. This control doesn't help against threat #1 (it assumes network access already exists) and doesn't fully protect against threat #3 (a privileged insider with broader rights than the application credential has).

3. A privileged insider (a DBA or admin with legitimate, broad access who misuses it, or whose credentials are compromised): this is specifically where Dynamic Data Masking and Always Encrypted matter, and specifically where they differ from each other in what they actually stop — DDM only prevents casual/accidental viewing by someone without UNMASK permission (a db_owner or sysadmin bypasses DDM entirely, so it does NOT protect against a privileged insider), whereas Always Encrypted on the SSN column specifically DOES protect against this threat, because the plaintext is never available to SQL Server or anyone querying it directly regardless of their SQL-level permissions — only the application, holding the actual encryption keys outside the database, can decrypt it. This is exactly why SSN specifically should be Always Encrypted, not just DDM-masked: DDM alone fails against this threat, Always Encrypted doesn't.

4. Data at rest theft (someone obtaining the physical database files/backups directly, bypassing the running SQL Server instance entirely): handled by Transparent Data Encryption, which encrypts the physical files/backups so that possessing the raw files without the TDE key yields nothing usable. This is irrelevant to threats #1-3, all of which involve going through the live SQL Server engine, not stealing files directly — TDE assumes the engine's own access controls (or their absence) aren't the attack vector; it protects a completely different attack surface.

5. After-the-fact audit/forensics (determining who accessed what, when, after an incident or for compliance reporting): handled by SQL Auditing (or Azure SQL Auditing to a storage account/Log Analytics), which records access events for later review. Critically, auditing is detective, not preventive — it does nothing to stop threats #1-4 from happening, it only provides the record needed to investigate after the fact, satisfy compliance reporting requirements, and potentially detect an in-progress misuse pattern if actively monitored.

No single control covers all five because each is designed to address a specific threat model and layer: network controls assume the threat is unauthorized connectivity; least-privilege/RLS assume the threat is a credential with too much reach; Always Encrypted assumes the threat is anyone with SQL-level read access including privileged ones; TDE assumes the threat bypasses SQL Server's access control entirely; and auditing assumes prevention already failed and focuses on detection/record-keeping. Removing any one layer leaves exactly the threat it was designed for completely unmitigated, regardless of how strong the other layers are.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through this threat by threat, because that's the only way to show why you actually need all five controls layered rather than picking 'the best one.'

For someone trying to reach the database who has no business being on the network at all, that's private endpoints and firewall rules — pure network-layer gatekeeping before authentication even enters the picture. That control is doing nothing for any of the other four threats; it only decides who gets to knock on the door.

For a compromised application credential, I'm leaning on least-privilege scoping — the app's identity should only be able to do exactly what the app needs — plus Row-Level Security if the real requirement is 'this context should only see these patients' records,' enforced at the engine level so even a cleverly-crafted query under that stolen credential can't read outside its lane.

For a privileged insider — this is where I have to be really precise, because Dynamic Data Masking and Always Encrypted sound similar but solve completely different problems. DDM does nothing against a db_owner or sysadmin — they bypass masking by design. Always Encrypted does protect against that threat, because the plaintext literally never exists inside SQL Server for anyone to see, privileged or not — only the application holding the real keys can decrypt it. That's exactly why something as sensitive as SSN needs Always Encrypted specifically, not just DDM.

For data at rest — someone walking off with the actual database files or backups, bypassing the running SQL Server entirely — that's Transparent Data Encryption's job, and it's doing something none of the above controls touch, because none of those assume the attacker skips the live engine altogether.

And for after-the-fact audit and forensics, that's SQL Auditing — and I always flag that this one is purely detective, not preventive. It doesn't stop anything from happening; it gives you the record to figure out what happened and prove compliance after the fact.

The reason you need all five, and why I'd push back on anyone who says 'just do Always Encrypted and call it done,' is that each of these assumes a different starting point for the attacker — network access or not, SQL-level access or not, engine-bypass or not, before or after the fact — and dropping any one of them leaves that specific starting point completely open, no matter how strong the rest of the stack is.
commonMistakes: Assuming Dynamic Data Masking protects against privileged insiders or DBAs
Believing TDE protects against anything happening through the live, authenticated SQL engine
Treating auditing as a preventive control rather than a detective one
Recommending only one or two controls as sufficient for all threat types
Not distinguishing which specific threat each control is actually designed to stop
keyPoints: Network controls (private endpoints/firewall) gate connectivity, independent of authentication/authorization
Least privilege + Row-Level Security limit the blast radius of a compromised application credential
Dynamic Data Masking does NOT protect against privileged insiders (db_owner/sysadmin bypass it)
Always Encrypted DOES protect against privileged insiders, since plaintext never exists inside SQL Server
Transparent Data Encryption protects against theft of physical files/backups, bypassing the engine entirely
SQL Auditing is detective (after the fact), not preventive, and doesn't stop any of the other four threats
Each control addresses a distinct layer/threat; removing any one leaves that specific threat unmitigated

Correctly distinguishes DDM's insider-threat limitation from Always Encrypted's insider protection
Correctly identifies auditing as detective, not preventive

questions.title: Designing an Elastic Jobs Maintenance Architecture for a Fleet of 300 Databases Across 6 Elastic Pools
questions.prompt: Design the Elastic Jobs architecture to run three different maintenance tasks — nightly statistics updates, weekly index maintenance, and monthly full-backup verification restores — across 300 databases spread over 6 elastic pools in 2 regions, with different teams owning different pools and wanting independent schedules and independent failure visibility per pool. Explain how target groups and job scoping let you avoid either 300 individually-managed jobs or one monolithic job nobody can safely change.
questions.modelAnswer:
The design principle is to decouple WHAT runs (the job step's T-SQL logic) from WHERE it runs (the target group) and WHEN it runs (the schedule), and to scope target groups at the pool level, one target group per elastic pool (6 target groups total), each one referencing its pool as a single target-group member rather than enumerating individual databases. This immediately gives each pool's databases dynamic membership (a new database added to a pool is automatically covered without editing anything) while keeping each pool's maintenance fully independent of the others.

For the three maintenance tasks, I'd create three separate job definitions (one for stats updates, one for index maintenance, one for backup-verification restores) rather than one combined job, specifically because they have genuinely different schedules (nightly, weekly, monthly) and different failure semantics worth tracking separately — a failed stats update overnight is a different severity/urgency than a failed backup-verification restore, and combining them into one job would blur that distinction in the job's own execution history.

For independent schedules and failure visibility PER POOL (the actual requirement, since different teams own different pools), each of the three job definitions gets instantiated once per target group it should apply to, rather than one job trying to cover all 6 pools' worth of target groups simultaneously with a single execution record — this means, for example, the nightly-stats job has 6 separate job/target-group pairings (one per pool), each with its own execution history in jobs.job_executions, so Team A can look at their pool's job history and failure alerts completely independently of Team B's pool, without either team's view being cluttered by or dependent on the other pool's results. If a team wants a different schedule for their pool's maintenance (say, Team A's weekly index maintenance runs Saturday, Team B's runs Sunday), that's a different schedule object attached to that pool's job pairing specifically, not a shared schedule forcing synchronization across teams who don't actually need it.

This target-group-per-pool, job-per-task structure avoids both failure modes in the question: it avoids 300 individually-managed jobs because membership within each pool's target group is automatic and dynamic, not manually enumerated per database; and it avoids one monolithic job nobody can safely change because each pool's job/target-group/schedule combination is independently modifiable — a team can adjust their own pool's schedule, add a new maintenance step, or investigate their own failure history without any risk of affecting another pool's maintenance, and because the three task types are separate job definitions, changing the index maintenance logic never risks breaking the unrelated stats-update or backup-verification jobs.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The structure I'd build this around is: one target group per elastic pool — six total — each one pointing at its pool as a single member rather than listing out every database by name, so membership inside each pool stays automatic as databases get added or removed. That alone avoids the '300 individually-managed jobs' trap, because I'm never touching individual database entries at all.

For the three maintenance tasks, I keep them as three separate job definitions rather than bundling everything into one job, because they run on different schedules and because I want their failure histories to stay distinct — a failed nightly stats update shouldn't get lost in the same execution log as a failed monthly backup-verification restore, those deserve different attention and different urgency.

The part that actually answers the 'independent per team' requirement is instantiating each of those three job definitions once per target group, rather than one job execution trying to cover all six pools at once. That gives each pool its own execution history for each task — Team A can look at just their pool's stats-update failures without wading through five other teams' results, and if Team A wants their index maintenance on Saturdays while Team B wants Sundays, that's just a different schedule object attached to that specific pool's job pairing, no synchronization required between teams who have no reason to be coupled together.

That's really the whole trick to avoiding both bad extremes here — I'm not managing 300 individual database-level jobs because pool-level target groups give me dynamic membership, and I'm not stuck with one giant job nobody wants to touch because each pool's job/schedule/target-group combination is its own independently-editable unit, and the three task types being separate jobs means touching one never risks breaking the other two.
commonMistakes: Enumerating individual databases in target groups instead of referencing the pool as a single member
Combining all three maintenance tasks into one job, losing independent schedule/failure tracking
Building one job execution meant to cover all 6 pools at once, blurring per-team failure visibility
Forcing all pools onto one shared schedule regardless of team ownership differences
Not recognizing that job/target-group/schedule separation is what enables independent modification per pool
keyPoints: One target group per elastic pool gives each pool dynamic, automatic database membership
Three separate job definitions (stats, index maintenance, backup verification) preserve distinct schedules and failure semantics
Instantiating each job once per target group gives per-pool independent execution history and failure visibility
Per-pool schedule objects allow different teams independent timing without cross-pool coupling
This structure avoids both 300 manually-managed jobs and one unmodifiable monolithic job

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs pool-level target groups for dynamic membership
Correctly separates the three maintenance tasks into distinct job definitions
Correctly designs per-pool job instantiation for independent schedules/failure visibility
Explains how this avoids both the 300-jobs and monolithic-job failure modes
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Designing an Index-Tuning Strategy at Scale Using Query Store and Automatic Tuning Together
questions.prompt: A platform has grown to 150 databases, too many to manually review execution plans on each one regularly. Design an index-tuning strategy that uses Query Store data collection and SQL Server's Automatic Tuning together across the fleet, explaining specifically what Automatic Tuning is allowed to do on its own without human approval, what it's not, and where a DBA's manual review still has to fit into the process despite the automation.
questions.modelAnswer:
At this scale, manual, per-database execution-plan review simply doesn't scale as a primary strategy — it has to become an exception-driven process layered on top of automation, not the default workflow for all 150 databases. The architecture has two tiers.

Tier one, automated: Query Store must be enabled (and sized/configured appropriately — retention period and capture policy tuned so it captures enough history without excessive storage overhead) on every database, since it's the data source Automatic Tuning depends on entirely; Automatic Tuning's FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN option can then be enabled fleet-wide, which specifically allows SQL Server to automatically detect a plan regression (a new plan performing meaningfully worse than a previous one for the same query, based on Query Store's own regression-verification logic) and automatically force the previously-known-good plan back, without any human approval in the loop — this directly addresses the most common, high-volume, low-judgment-required case (yesterday's plan was fine, today's isn't, revert) at a scale no DBA team could manually track across 150 databases. Automatic Tuning can also (depending on edition/configuration) automatically create and validate missing index recommendations, but critically, automatic INDEX creation is a more consequential, schema-level change than reverting to a known-good plan, and Azure SQL's own automatic tuning for index management includes built-in verification (it monitors the created index's actual impact and will automatically drop it if it doesn't deliver the expected improvement) — this is a meaningfully different risk profile from plan forcing, and a DBA should know whether index-create automation is enabled fleet-wide or being left to recommendation-only mode (CREATE_INDEX recommendations surfaced for review, versus auto-applied), as a deliberate choice, not a default nobody examined.

What Automatic Tuning is NOT allowed to do, and where manual review still fits: it doesn't redesign a bad data model, rewrite a non-SARGable query, recognize that an index is redundant with another existing index (only that a new one would help a specific query pattern, without necessarily considering fleet-wide redundancy across many similar queries), or make a judgment call about a deliberate, known trade-off (an index that helps one report but measurably slows a high-frequency write path elsewhere) — those require human judgment about trade-offs the automation isn't positioned to weigh. So tier two, manual: a DBA's actual recurring job at this scale shifts to exception-driven review — regularly reviewing the Automatic Tuning recommendations/history dashboard (and Query Store's own top-resource-consumer views) across the fleet for patterns worth a deeper look, specifically looking for: databases where Automatic Tuning is firing unusually often (suggesting a deeper, recurring problem automation is band-aiding rather than fixing), index recommendations flagged but not auto-applied (left for human judgment specifically because of their consequence level), and periodic spot-checks of the fleet's worst-performing queries by resource consumption, using Query Store's aggregated cross-database view, rather than trying to review every database's plans on a fixed schedule regardless of whether anything's actually wrong there.
questions.professionalAnswer:
At 150 databases, I stop thinking of execution-plan review as something I do proactively on a schedule across every database, and start thinking of it as something automation handles by default, with my actual job being to review the exceptions automation surfaces.

The automated tier starts with Query Store enabled everywhere, since it's the actual data source everything else depends on, sized sensibly for retention. Then I'd turn on Automatic Tuning's force-last-good-plan behavior fleet-wide — that's the piece that can detect 'this query's new plan is measurably worse than its old one' and just revert to the known-good plan automatically, no human in the loop, which is exactly the high-volume, low-judgment case that doesn't scale if I'm trying to catch it manually across 150 databases.

Index creation I treat with more caution, because that's a bigger, schema-level change than just forcing a plan back. Azure SQL's automatic index management does have its own built-in safety net — it watches whether a new index it created is actually helping and drops it automatically if it isn't — but I still want to make a deliberate decision about whether auto-create is actually turned on fleet-wide versus just surfacing recommendations for me to review, rather than that being some default nobody actually looked at.

What I'm clear-eyed about is everything this automation can't do — it's not going to notice a redundant index sitting next to another one that does almost the same job, it's not going to rewrite a badly-written non-SARGable query, and it's definitely not going to weigh a trade-off like 'this index helps one report but slows down a high-frequency write path' — that needs a human looking at it with real context. So my actual recurring job becomes reviewing the automatic tuning history and recommendation dashboard across the fleet looking for patterns — which databases are triggering this unusually often, which index recommendations got flagged but not auto-applied, and periodically spot-checking the worst resource consumers fleet-wide through Query Store's aggregated view, instead of trying to eyeball every database's plans on some fixed rotation whether or not anything's actually wrong there.
commonMistakes: Trying to manually review execution plans on all 150 databases on a fixed schedule
Assuming Automatic Tuning can safely redesign queries or recognize cross-index redundancy
Enabling automatic index creation fleet-wide without a deliberate decision about the risk trade-off
Believing Automatic Tuning eliminates the need for any human review at this scale
Not leveraging Query Store's own regression-verification logic before assuming force-last-good-plan is risky
keyPoints: Query Store must be enabled/configured on every database as the data source Automatic Tuning depends on
FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN automatically reverts plan regressions without human approval
Automatic index creation carries higher risk than plan forcing, though Azure SQL verifies and can auto-drop ineffective indexes
Automatic Tuning cannot redesign data models, rewrite non-SARGable queries, or judge cross-query trade-offs
The DBA's role shifts to exception-driven review of tuning history/recommendations, not per-database manual plan review
Fleet-wide aggregated Query Store views support periodic spot-checks of worst resource consumers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the two-tier (automated + exception-driven manual) architecture
Correctly explains FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN's automatic, no-approval-needed scope
Correctly explains the higher risk profile and verification behavior of automatic index creation
Correctly identifies what Automatic Tuning cannot do, requiring human judgment
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Managed Instance vs. Azure SQL Database for a Legacy On-Prem Migration
questions.prompt: A client's on-prem SQL Server application relies on cross-database queries, SQL Server Agent jobs, Service Broker, and CLR integration. They want to move to Azure with minimal application rewrite. Walk through why Azure SQL Managed Instance is very likely the right target over Azure SQL Database, tying each specific feature they depend on to why Managed Instance supports it and plain Azure SQL Database does not (or supports it only in a limited form).
questions.modelAnswer:
Each of the four dependencies the client has maps directly to an instance-scoped SQL Server capability that Azure SQL Database, as a single-database PaaS offering, either doesn't support at all or supports only in a constrained way, while Managed Instance, as a near-full-surface-area instance-level PaaS offering, supports natively:

Cross-database queries (three-part naming, querying across databases on the same instance): Azure SQL Database is architected as an isolated single-database (or elastic-pool-of-databases) unit — there is no shared instance context across databases the way on-prem SQL Server has, so cross-database three-part-name queries are not supported at all between separate Azure SQL databases (you'd need Elastic Query or application-side federation, which requires rewriting that logic, not a drop-in replacement). Managed Instance, by contrast, is explicitly instance-scoped — multiple databases exist within one Managed Instance and can be queried cross-database with standard three-part naming exactly as on-prem, because Managed Instance was specifically designed to preserve this instance-level surface area.

SQL Server Agent jobs: Azure SQL Database has no SQL Server Agent at all (Azure SQL Database uses Elastic Jobs instead, a different, database-scoped automation mechanism requiring jobs to be rewritten against a different API/stored-procedure surface). Managed Instance includes a real SQL Server Agent, so existing jobs can be migrated with little to no rewriting, directly satisfying 'minimal application rewrite.'

Service Broker: Azure SQL Database does not support Service Broker for message exchange between different databases (very limited/no support), since Service Broker's architecture assumes a shared instance context for routing messages between databases, similar to the cross-database query limitation. Managed Instance supports Service Broker within the instance, again because it preserves that instance-level architecture.

CLR integration: Azure SQL Database does not support SQLCLR at all. Managed Instance supports CLR integration, closely matching on-prem capability, because Managed Instance runs on a fuller SQL Server engine surface rather than the more restricted PaaS single-database engine.

The general pattern an interviewer wants to hear articulated: Azure SQL Database trades away instance-level features (cross-database anything, Agent, Service Broker, CLR, and others like linked servers) in exchange for being a more fully-managed, lighter-weight single-database PaaS service; Managed Instance is positioned specifically to preserve near-complete instance-level SQL Server surface area while still being a PaaS offering (automated patching, backups, HA built in), which is exactly why 'minimal application rewrite' for an app built assuming instance-level features points toward Managed Instance, not Azure SQL Database, even though Azure SQL Database is often the simpler, cheaper default recommendation for a fresh application with no such dependencies.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Every single thing this client depends on is actually an instance-level feature, not a single-database feature, and that's the whole reason I'd steer them toward Managed Instance instead of plain Azure SQL Database.

Cross-database queries first — Azure SQL Database doesn't have a shared instance context the way on-prem does; each database is its own isolated unit, so three-part-name queries across databases just don't work there without rewriting that logic through something like Elastic Query. Managed Instance keeps the instance-level model, so cross-database queries work exactly like they did on-prem.

SQL Server Agent is the same story — Azure SQL Database doesn't have Agent at all, it has Elastic Jobs instead, which is a genuinely different system requiring real rework. Managed Instance has actual SQL Server Agent, so existing jobs come across close to as-is.

Service Broker leans on that same shared-instance architecture for routing messages between databases, which Azure SQL Database doesn't really support, while Managed Instance does, again because it's preserving that instance-level surface.

And CLR — Azure SQL Database just doesn't support SQLCLR, full stop. Managed Instance does.

So the pattern I'd point out to the client is: Azure SQL Database made a deliberate trade — give up instance-level features in exchange for being leaner, simpler, fully single-database-managed PaaS. Managed Instance made the opposite trade — keep almost all of that instance-level SQL Server surface area, while still being a managed PaaS service with automated patching and built-in HA. Given everything this application actually depends on, Managed Instance is clearly the target that gets them to 'minimal rewrite' — Azure SQL Database would mean rewriting four separate pieces of existing functionality just to get in the door.
commonMistakes: Recommending Azure SQL Database by default without checking for instance-level feature dependencies
Assuming Elastic Jobs is a drop-in replacement for SQL Server Agent requiring no rewrite
Not knowing Azure SQL Database lacks CLR support entirely
Assuming Service Broker or cross-database queries work the same way on Azure SQL Database as on-prem
Failing to tie each specific client dependency to the specific reason Managed Instance supports it
keyPoints: Azure SQL Database is architecturally single-database-scoped; it lacks shared instance context
Cross-database three-part-name queries require Elastic Query (a rewrite) on Azure SQL Database; native on Managed Instance
Azure SQL Database has no SQL Server Agent (uses Elastic Jobs instead); Managed Instance has real Agent
Azure SQL Database does not support Service Broker; Managed Instance does
Azure SQL Database does not support SQLCLR at all; Managed Instance does
Managed Instance trades some PaaS simplicity to preserve near-full instance-level SQL Server surface area

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains cross-database query limitation on Azure SQL DB vs. Managed Instance support
Correctly explains SQL Server Agent absence vs. Elastic Jobs vs. Managed Instance support
Correctly explains Service Broker limitation vs. Managed Instance support
Correctly explains CLR unsupported on Azure SQL DB vs. supported on Managed Instance
Articulates the general architectural trade-off pattern clearly
